Mr. Speaker, I have the privilege today to respond to the motion moved by the hon. member concerning the action taken by our government in order to reduce the unemployment rate among young Canadians. I totally agree with my hon. colleague that we need to do everything in our power to help young Canadians find a job. And I would like to specifically address the situation of our youth in the Montreal area.
Since its first election in 1984, our government has worked hard to encourage young Canadians to pursue their studies, to realize their full academic potential and, once they graduated, to find a motivating job that would represent their contribution to Canadian productivity.
Of course, the hon. member knows, as we all know, that the present economic situation is difficult, not only in Canada, but in all industrialized countries. Despite that, our youth show initiative and, far from getting discouraged, they show entrepreneurship, which will certainly have the effect of raising the standard of living of Canadians during the present decade and even during the twenty-first centuiy.
Our government does all it can to support their efforts. Indeed, it is the seventh summer that we put in place the Challenge Program, which is under the jurisdiction of the Minister of State for Youth and whose aim is to encourage employers to create interesting summer jobs for young people. The future of young Canadians is at the forefront of government priorities. I believe we have proved it when we announced this year that $143
million would go into the Challenge Program 91. That is $3 million more than in last year's budget.
Also, of these $143 million, $28.3 million will go to Challenge 91 for Quebec. Let me explain to the hon. member the components of that program. One of the components of the Challenge Program is called Summer Employment Experience Development (SEED). It assists employers by giving them salary subsidies that will allow them to create jobs for secondary school, college and university students, but especially for secondary school students who have more difficulty than others to find a job.
The hon. member will be happy to learn that in the Montreal area, last summer, our government spent more than $4 million under this component and, more precisely, that 2,655 students participated in 1,146 projects over-all, which allowed them to receive a valuable training while earning money to continue their education.
I am pleased to tell the hon. member that this year again, the SEED component will encourage the creation of job opportunities conforming to government social priorities in the areas of literacy, drug and alcohol abuse, information on AIDS, environment, and urban crime.
Moreover, the funding of SEED this year is aimed at encouraging employers to hire visible minorities, natives and young handicapped.
In Quebec, the funds allocated to this program will be increased this summer from $17.8 million to $18.1 million. My hon. friend will certainly understand that summer has just started and that we do not quite know yet how many students from Montreal schools will participate in this program. There is ground to believe that this component of Challenge 91 will have as much success as in previous summers.
The Challenge program includes also a component called Work Orientation Workshops that gives high school dropouts an opportunity to reconsider their decision to not complete their education. These workshops are accompanied by an on-the-job experience aimed at encouraging dropout students to go back to school or, if they do not want to, to receive a practical training. More precisely, these workshops teach life dynamics, personal financial management, the operation of companies, and so on. These workshops help young people to understand what training and studies they will need to get in the labour market, where jobs require more and more skills and are more specialized.
June 10, 1991

I am pleased to be able to tell my honourable colleague, that as of the summer of 1990, the government had given the Montreal area more than $2 million through the Work Orientation Workshops, and 1,000 area students took part in them. For instance, on the South Shore only, $920,000 were spent on 467 participants.
This summer, the Quebec component of the Work Orientation Workshops will receive a total of $8.1 million, over and above a supplementary $2.1 million for year-round projects.
On May 9th, the Minister of State for Youth officially opened for the summer the 94 Canada Employment Centres for Students that are to be found in Quebec. Four of these centres are in the Montreal area. I can assure my honourable colleague that employees in these centres know full well how hard it is for young people in Montreal to find a job and that they use all their skills to help them.
As I was saying a while ago, everyone here knows that the whole world is going through very difficult economic times. Nevertheless, I am sure that the members of this House will recognize that the situation would be far worse for young Canadians were it not for the efficient assistance programs brought forth by this government. I am not only talking about the conponents of Challenge '91 I have just mentioned, but also about a few others such as the Student Business Loans Program which is administered by the Federal Business Development Bank and assits student entrepreneurs who wish to create their own summer jobs.
Last year in Quebec, 276 loans were approved for a total of $688,700 which led to the creation of 918 summer jobs. This is a sizeable increase of 72 per cent compared with the number of jobs created the previous year. And this year, this component has an over-all operating budget of $900,000. Moreover, we will grant $805,000 more for the Business Drive for Jobs component under which business associations are encouraged to create summer jobs for students within the business community without the help of salary subsidies.
We have also established the Native probationers Program which is offered during the summer and give
Supply
native students the oppurtunity to work in Employment and Immigration offices.
Mr. Speaker, by taking advantage of Challenge '91 Program, employers in Montreal and across Canada will have a unique opportunity to raise the potential of our future Canadian labour force. For students, as for other young people, the Challenge' 91 components meet a periode range of employment needs including help for students who want to start a business and counselling to younger students who hesitate between staying in school and joining the work force.
Our action is an attempt at helping young people from Montreal and from all over the country, choose between their staying in school or going into the labour market. Our programs are intented to prepare our youths for employment. However, we should never go so far as to tell our young people to get a job instead of finishing school. That is why our government implemented its stay-in-school initiative in February 1990. Over five years, this project should receive $296 million. There is an alarming 30 per cent drop-out rate in Canada at the high school level. That rate could well be the highest in all of the industrialized world. My hon. colleague will recognize, I am sure, that this figure has to be checked.
Mr. Speaker, we all know that, by the year 2000, for two thirds of all new jobs, candidates will be required to have at least a high school diploma and, in many cases, five years of post-secondary schooling.
Students who drop out of school will earn much less than those with a high school degree and will have a much harder time finding and keeping a job. School drop-outs will be unemployed for longer periods of time than other workers. Either they will have to accept low-paid, low-skill jobs or make do with unemployment or some other type of income support. We must not let such a thing happen, and this government is committed to do everything possible to help youths in Montreal and across the country develop their intellectual potential.
Of course, we know that lack of education is an obstacle, and not only on a personal level. It can also translate into a much heavier burden on public assistance programs during a severe recession as the one we are experiencing now.

June 10, 1991
Supply
We must also ask ourselves what will happen if the dropout rate remains at 30 per cent. Who will fill the new jobs requiring sound training if we do not have a sufficient number of skilled workers to fill these jobs? How will Canada compete in the rapidly growing global economy?
The Stay-in-School project not only enhances access to well-paying jobs for a lifetime, it helps youths to accede to a better quality life. It gets us wondering: who should help defining these problems and finding solutions?
The answer lies in the three components of the project, that is programs and services related to labour market and geared to students at risk of dropping out of school, mobilization of stakeholders in order to find solutions, and public awareness activities to inform Canadians on the consequences of the current dropout rate.
Of course, education comes under the responsibility of the provinces, and we fully respect their prerogative in that area. However, my honourable colleague will surely agree with me that the long term consequences of dropout could affect the whole economy of this country, and that, to curb the problem, we have to combine our efforts on a national level.
That is why we call upon all those affected by this problem: parents, union leaders, social groups, young Canadians, business people and teachers. We need the opinion of all those involved because they know better than we do the problems affecting their communities.
During the last fiscal year, we added to the Stay-inSchool project a new component called Start Option. It is a $16 million program that gives financial assistance , for projects aimed at young people from 12 to 18 years of age.
Start Option is financed through the Job Entry Program of the Canadian Job Strategy and offers considerable flexibility. It allows organizations which qualify for the program, such as school boards, Indian bands and youth-oriented organizations, to receive funds in order to encourage young people to stay in school.
In the same vein, I have the pleasure to be able to point to my hon. colleague that, during the last fiscal year, Quebec joined the Stay-in-School project. A total
of $1.5 million, including $153,000 for the mobilization of stake-holders will be spent in Quebec under Start Option.
For example, last summer, in Montreal, ten drop-outs were sponsored by the YMCA du Parc under Start Option, and they all went back to school this year.
Furthermore, last year in Quebec the Canadian Jobs Strategy's job entry program received funding totalling nearly $3.3 million, which benefited 176 participants.
I would like to give you and the hon. member for Welland-St. Catharines-Thorold the assurance that this government is doing everything it can, in Montreal as well as in the rest of Quebec and Canada, to help young Canadians become productive citizens.
When we adopted our Labour Force Development Strategy two years ago, our aim was to consolidate programs that promote the social integration of young people. Thanks to this strategy, our Co-operative Education Program has become even more accessible in high schools and universities across Canada. The program, which is very popular, gives students an opportunity to combine education and job experience, and we are committed to increasing funding for this very important program.
The Labour Force Development Strategy has led to an increase in entry-level skills development and has helped direct young unemployed workers towards the programs and services they need to find work. By further developing co-operative education, by improving apprenticeship programs and by emphasizing a comprehensive and concrete approach to entry-level skills development, we are giving young Canadians the kind of training they need to find a niche in a very competitive labour market. The government is using all these programs and initiatives to try and improve training and job opportunities for young Canadians.
Last year, the Science Council of Canada published a report in which it said that to sustain international competition, it was necessary to co-operate at the national level. That is what the government does. It creates partnerships with business, unions, the provinces and social agencies. A recent example is the $7.4 million the government has committed, over a period of three years, to research and development in the field of counselling methods and training programs for counsellors.
June 10, 1991

Our emphasis on partnerships is also apparent every fall during Canada Career Week. Special events organized across the country, with the co-operation of Canada Employment Centres, schools and business, give young people a chance to find out more about various occupations and think about their career choices. This fall, Canada Career Week will focus on younger students and urge them to start thinking about their careers.
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Welland-St. Catharines-Thorold knows as well as we do that Canada can no longer count on human resources alone to make its economy prosper. In the last Speech from the Throne, the government clearly indicated that in a global economy, prosperity depends increasingly on knowledge, skills and innovation. That is why we emphasize up-dating skills so that young Canadians can develop and diversify our economy and give us a head start on world markets. Business, unions and governments are invited to work together to create at least 2.5 million new jobs by the year 2000 and to increase the real income of Canadians by at least 25 per cent.
Mr. Speaker, these objectives are realistic, but our young people will have the difficult task of achieving them. I want to give the hon. member the assurance that through the programs and initiatives I just described, this government, in co-operation with its partners in Montreal, Quebec and Canada as a whole, is trying to transform a national co-operative effort into effective local action. We are doing everything we can to provide a brilliant future for young Canadians, and we mean all young Canadians.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate my hon. colleague on this excellent speech and let him know that, no later than tomorrow, I will make sure, and it is my duty, that everyone involved

in school issues in my riding gets a copy of this historic speech.
Mr. Speaker, in the discharge of my duties over the past seven years, I have often met people, men and women, who were looking for a job, either because they had lost their job or wanted a change. In every case, I did the same thing. I tried to make them realize that nobody is in a better position than they are to help them find a job. As the saying goes: "God helps those who help themselves." I noticed that they do not always give themselves every chance of succeeding. That is when I believe my advice can be the useful and, to sum it up, Mr. Speaker, my advice is this: first, identify the position that suits you before applying; concentrate on employers in the chosen field; apply in person; preferably, have a clear and up to date resume; finally, take great care over your presentation at the time of the interview.
These constitute, Mr. Speaker, the ABC of success in job hunting. In my experience, a highly motivated person almost always finds work within a reasonable time, provided of course that person puts in the time and energy required and does not rely exclusively on others to do it for him or her.
From what my hon. colleague from Bourassa just said,
I am convinced she pays as much attention to the young people in search of a job in her riding as I do in mine and gives them more or less the same advice.
I would like to ask the hon. member for Bourassa a specific question on the excellent, as I said earlier, speech she just gave. We know that the Co-operative ' Education program is a success wherever it is implemented across Canada. Can the federal government provide increased funding for this program?

Mr. Speaker, this particular program, which is also part of the Labour Force Development Strategy, has been quite successful. Since it was introduced, $9 million per year has been spent on co-operative education. Furthermore, the government has approved new commitments totalling $16 million for the next four years to promote the co-opera-

June 10,1991
Supply
tive education concept. High school students remain and always will be a major concern of this government. As you know, they are the labour force of the twenty-first centuiy. Since this particular group happens to be the worst off at this time, the government is going to do everything it can to help bridge the transition between education and work.
In its comments, the opposition asked us to show some original thinking, to show initiative and creativity. I hope our colleagues on the other side of the House realize the tremendous range of programs that our government introduced since it came to power. The Challenge Program, for instance, which did not exist before and was introduced in 1985, almost seven years ago, a program that has a number of components such as Summer Employment Experience Development, Work Orientation Workshops, Student Business Loans, Business Drive for Jobs, CECs for Students, and Native Internship Programs. There are plenty of programs to help young people deal with the kind of situations they can expect.
I realize the situation is not a particularly easy one. In fact, we have a very critical situation, but our government has decided to face the facts and do what has to be done to ensure that the present critical situation with respect to youth employment will not be merely postponed, to be faced by future generations. In fact, what we see today was predictable a number of years ago. Without trying to blame anyone, however, we have decided to implement the necessary strategies to ensure that the problems we are able to identify now and to which we intend to respond will not be carried on to the next generation.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the hon. member for Bourassa for her excellent speech describing all the initiatives and programs the government has put in place to help young Canadians get a good education in with a view to securing a job later on.
I know the hon. member for Bourassa is very concerned by the situation in Montreal and today's debate must really be of interest to her. I would therefore like to ask her the following question. Given the serious problem of young people who drop out of school because they do not think they will find a job, if she were a student today in Montreal, what message would she convey to
students who are thinking of dropping out? What advice could she give them?

Mr. Speaker, that is a very good question. Actually, even though we have a full load of answers for them, the only advice we can give them are alternatives, through all our programs. So, as my hon. colleague said not too long ago, the only thing we can tell them is this: every generation, be it our very own, the previous one or the following one, every generation complains about being society's sacrificial lamb every one of them. The same goes for today's youth. They think of themselves somewhat as victims.
Last week, a young man in my constituency told me he could not see any reason to stay in school. He blamed his parents and the previous generation for having been too tolerant. I thought that was funny, because when we were young, we blamed our parents, our teachers or previous generations for some other wrongdoings.
It is never easy to be young. Kids have to take matters into their own hands, although they have been overly-protected and pampered, as is the case with the present generation. The reason they are going through all this might be that their parents and grand-parents, like my own, having lived through the war, became very strict. And then the people from my generation decided to try something else and we became much more tolerant.
The advice I would give them is first of all to be proud of their country. When one looks at the Japanese, one can admire the pride they show in everything they do. That could be considered chauvinistic, but perhaps the time has come to talk about that. The other advice I would give them is that there is certainly no future in dropping out, nor in giving up, nor in refusing to take up a challenge. The future is theirs. Indeed, it is an exciting challenge and it is all the more so because it is difficult. So I would advise them to complete their education because there is no other alternative. There will be absolutely no work for them without basic qualifications. Whether it be at the secondary or postsecondary level, there is no job for underqualified people.
Increasingly, with technological advances and market globalization, the fierce and sound competition which will prevail because of the opening up and rationalization of the Canadian people, our young people, will have to become more productive, more efficient and more qualified at any level and in any field. They have no alternative but to stay in school.
June 10, 1991

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to be able to address this particular motion because it is one that is of particular importance to Canadians generally, and certainly to young Canadians.
Members will recall that last Tuesday the Minister of State for Finance said in this House if they, that is students, look hard enough for jobs they will find them. Because the minister had said it, I thought perhaps I should check it out. Last Saturday in my constituency I took a young man and we went around to see what was available.

He is a good-looking young man, has good marks in school and is just finishing high school. He is motivated, has a number of skills and it seems to me he could be very useful in many areas. He is good-mannered and proud, he loves to work and has excellent credentials.
We visited eleven places like family restaurants, groceries, hardware stores, and so on. He did not get the slightest chance to have a job offer. He was told everywhere that there was no opening for the time being. There was no opening for the time being, and probably no opening during the week, the next week or the summer months.
Now, that is only one example of what is happening throughout this country. I intend to try the same kind of experience next Saturday. I will go around a number of other sectors with a young woman to see whether she has any chance to get a job.
Mr. Speaker, I must tell you that that young man I was just talking about had made a few written applications. We went to perhaps half the places where he had made an application.
Now, my colleague just said, and I appreciate her comments, that the government is doing all it can. But that is simply not good enough!

There is, not on the part of all members, but on the part of certain members in government, an insensitive
Supply
attitude. "If they look hard enough for them, they will find them". I think that is too facile. That is too superficial. It is not that easy. What annoys me and young Canadians throughout the country is that there is no acknowledgement of the problem. If you cannot acknowledge that there is a problem, then how can you possibly deal with it?
This government has talked incessantly of competitiveness. We have to be competitive. That means what? That means, obviously, education, training and retraining. Clearly, we would all acknowledge that one is also educated through work. If I look at my particular life in the workplace and in schools, colleges and universities, I think I have learned as much in the workplace as I have in those formal institutions.
Why talk of competitiveness in such glowing terms with such rhetoric, when we see that the follow-up is not there, that there is tremendous disappointment on the part of young people?

That is what the situation is today among our young people. When we look at transfer payments for post-secondary education, the provinces will receive billions of dollars less. For training and retraining, we all know that less funds are allocated while more people need to be trained or retrained.
When we look at assistance to students, we see that the criteria have not changed since 1984. When it comes to programs for part-time students, everybody knows, including the government, that it is a disaster. We know that the number of part-time students has increased considerably. Then we have the 3 per cent administrative charge imposed on student loans; a 3 per cent charge for students who are the poorest, and we have not yet spoken of the GST on books and other learning material. You know very well that students are getting more and more heavily indebted. It is appalling and scary! It frightens those young people.
If we look at tuition fees, for instance, in my own province, since 1985, there has been an increase of almost 80 per cent. Those are the facts. Let us now talk of this job program for students.

June 10, 1991
Supply

Summer employment funding from 1985 to 1990, we recognize that the program has been reduced, cut, call it what you like, there is less money, from $149 million to $77 million, a cut of $69 million.
It is true that in February of this year the former Minister of State for Youth said: "Because of difficult economic times", referring to the recession, "we will put in another $3 million". It is not particularly difficult to put in $3 million when you have already cut a program by almost $70 million.
I could reduce all of my employees' wages by one-half, which is approximately the cut, and then give them a 3 or 4 per cent increase, and I am sure that they would not be particularly impressed.
What has been the result of all of this? There were 40,115 fewer jobs than in 1985, if one compares the 1990 total with that of 1985. In fact, there were fewer jobs in 1990 than there were in the year 1985. The average length of those jobs was 9.5 weeks in 1990 and the average wage was $6.10 per hour. That gives you the grand total, possibly, of roughly $2,300 per summer job per student. If you look at the increase in tuition fees that I have been mentioning, add no changes in student aid since 1984, increases in rent and all of their amenities of life, the 3 per cent administrative fee, the GST on various goods and what have you, clearly these students are working in an extremely difficult environment.
There has also been another problem that we have not yet talked about and we must address it. Initially, the intent was to have career-oriented jobs to really help with the learning, to help develop certain skills, to refine them if you wish, to make them more marketable, more competitive. Well, unfortunately, a lot of that has slipped by the wayside, and we do not have the same focus, we do not have the same commitment, or, at least, the intended results are not being produced. That is really unfortunate.
Let me just give another figure. If you look at the wages today and compare them with those of 1985 you see an increase of 12 per cent. So, if one looks at inflation during that period of time, roughly 20 per cent, there has been a net decrease in wages for students.
Now let us look at the unemployment statistics. They are in the range of 20 per cent. If one compares May of this year with May of last year, there is 4.4 per cent more student unemployment this year in the 15 to 24 year-old range, which is really unfortunate. Of course, the 20 per cent range camouflages a whole lot of things because in areas such as Montreal and, I suspect, Newfoundland and the Territories, it is probably a whole lot higher.
What is needed? A complete review of this program and all student-related programs is needed in order to ensure that they respond to student needs in terms of economic and social development priorities. We need wide input and we need to involve the students.

Mr. Speaker, I don't deny that the government made a number of efforts. Yet we have to ask the basic question: Do we meet student needs? If our young men and women loose hope, if they begin to think that they can no longer find jobs and that they can no longer hope for a promising future, I think that Canada and all Canadians are loosing something.

Let us make sure that our young men and women of this nation are, in fact, the priority, that there are jobs, meaningful and significant jobs, to help them develop their skills, their abilities, their potential. Let us make sure that they do not despair, that they get the learning experiences that they need in order to make a contribution to this country.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the previous speaker, the member for St. Boniface, a question as it relates to the situation back in the early eighties when unemployment was extremely high in this country, along with an inflation rate that was rapidly increasing, and bank interest rates were very, very high.
This motion before us really does not give any alternative or make any particular suggestions other than to condemn the good work that is being done. In light of this, I would like to ask the member for St. Boniface if he has some suggestions, maybe reflecting on his experiences in the early eighties, as to how to improve the present unemployment situation. What particular things would this member like to see happening for Canadian youth in the employment sector?
June 10, 1991

I thank the hon. member for the question. I want to make sure I have understood the question because I think that my colleague was referring to the world recession in 1981-82, as opposed to the made-in-Canada recession of today, where indeed there were serious difficulties: interest rates and high unemployment. Absolutely. He failed to mention, of course, the differences in interest rates between Canada and the U.S. which recently have been at a record high. But we will set that aside for the time being.
I am amazed because I really did not simply point out the difficulties and pitfalls and some of the weaknesses of the programs. I did that because I expect that the government would want to listen to what it is that we have to say because it might be able to benefit from that. One of the main points I made is that there should be a total review of those programs to see if they are indeed in line with the government's economic and social development policies.
That was the first point. The second point was that there should be wide consultations in order to ensure that the review is as comprehensive, sensible and sensitive as possible. I did mention as well that it would be important to have the students involved in that kind of review.
With respect to money, because that is obviously an important consideration, we have a deficit of $30 billion and it has been hovering around that number for a long, long time. It will soon be $400 billion. It has more than doubled over the last seven years. I know we have a serious economic problem.
When I look at these cuts of $69 million and I look at some of the other activities the government undertakes, I cannot help but wonder whether we would not have been able to maintain such a program. Perhaps we would have been able to enhance it.
When there was a war in the gulf, money was found to go to war. We ought to be launching war against poverty; we ought to be launching war against unemployment; we ought to be making certain that our young people have the skills and the experience so they can contribute fully to Canada. I know that is what he wants, and certainly that is what I want. That is what my party wants.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for St. Boniface and I just returned from the opening of the Assembly of First Nations conference in Winnipeg. My hon. friend comes from a province with a very large portion of aboriginal people. He will recall that just a year or so ago the government cut the funding for post-secondary education to Indians.
I would like to ask him about this. He comes from a province with a very high number of aboriginal people. I would like to ask him about the devastating impact on young aboriginal people, young Indians, young Metis, and how that is going to affect their whole outlook on life.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank my colleague for the question. I tried to address that in part. Certainly his question is much more specific.
As I pointed out, unemployment figures for people 15 to 24 years of age are, as of this May, 4.4 per cent higher compared to a year ago. There are pockets within Canada where it is alarmingly high.
I was told as recently as last night, when my hon. friend and I attended the same function in Winnipeg with respect to the outgoing Chief Erasmus, that there are unemployment figures of over 90 per cent on our reserves. How can our young aboriginal people have any hope for the future when they face such a debilitating kind of situation? C'est ecrasant, c'est extraordinaire.

Mr. Speaker, in this motion which we have put before the House, we are calling on the government to implement immediately measures to alleviate the devastatingly high rate of unemployment among Canadian youth.
If we look at the unemployment figures which came out last Friday, the rate of unemployment for youth in this country in May was 16.6 per cent. That figure covers youth who are going to return to university, to CEGEP or to college in the fall and it also includes non-student youth. The figure of 16.6 per cent is considerably higher than the 10.3 per cent which is the general unemployment rate in this country, and that is bad enough; nearly
1.5	million Canadians unemployed. However, if you break down the figure of 16.6 per cent unemployment for youth, it is 15.8 per cent for students who will return to school and to university and it is 17.4 per cent for non-student youth.

June 10,1991
Supply
Look at some of the things that are being said about this. I have here a clipping from The Globe and Mail dated June 4, 1991. The headline reads: "Thirsting for employment in the summer job drought. Summer jobs for university students are drying up while tuition fees are rising and students are becoming more serious about finding work related to their fields of study. The situation has made some students bitter, while others are close to panic." The article goes on to say that many of the jobs are part time or casual and the wages are near to the minimum wage.
Students rely on summer employment to pay their tuition, lodgings, food and books, and to live during the year while they are in university.
I have another article, this one from The Montreal Gazette of May 21. It is on the youth unemployment situation in Montreal, particularly with respect to students and their attempts to find summer jobs. It talks of one student who is among the 1,700 university graduates in Montreal who this year will find themselves jumping into a job market already made sluggish by a recession and a local unemployment rate which has left as many as
200,000	people seeking work in Montreal.
In the French newspapers, we see in La Presse [Translation]
-May 27 1991: Tough summer for the students. The unemployment rate for those aged between 15 and 24 dramatically increased since September, that is less than a year, from 13.9 per cent last year to 20.9 per cent this year in Montreal. This summer, many students will have to accept small jobs paying the minimum wage.
Mr. Speaker, we could also read the following in an Ottawa newspaper, Le Droit, on April 25: Youth unemployment Statistics Canada just announced that youth unemployment in Quebec has reached alarming levels. Last month, the unemployment rate for those aged between 15 and 24 reached almost 21 per cent, that is 7 per cent more than March of last year.

This situation is alarming and what is the government's response? Two years ago the government cut the summer employment program, the Challenge program, by 35 per cent and this year it was increased by a mere $3 million, an increase of 2.5 per cent, I believe. With unemployment becoming a larger and larger problem,
that was total nonsense. Total nonsense in face of the problem.
The hon. member just asked a question of my colleague: what would you do? What we would do is put the funding back where it was in 1984, 1985 and 1986 so that community groups and small businesses could employ people to do the jobs that have to be done.
In my own constituency, for example, the Challenge program has been cut for four consecutive years. Last year the funding was $107,865; this year it is $89,677, a cut of 20 per cent. Last year we were able to fund 68 jobs, this year only 50.1 have already described the unemployment figures for students in Montreal.
What would we do? The groups that have lost those jobs are day care centres for young people. These are programs to help the elderly in hospitals and in senior citizens' homes. These are jobs in hospitals and in rehabilitation centres. If the government had a little more political will and put the money up front, there are all sorts of things that have to be done in this country, especially by social agencies for the poor, the sick, the elderly and for impoverished youth. Those jobs are there waiting to be funded. The government is simply backing off with this ridiculous argument that because we have a deficit we must cut back on all things. It is cutting back on the wrong things. The last thing you cut back on in time of recession is education and helping young people prepare for education.
What has the government done? It has not only cut back on the programs for summer employment. In the last budget it cut back on the training and retraining programs. It cut back on assistance to the provinces for post-secondary education. It cut back and closed the student employment centres and it cut back on research and development. These are the last things that you will ever cut because these are the things that help you increase your national income and productivity. These are the things that create a thriving economy.
If you do not have trained, skilled workers, if you do not have the professional people, the scientists, to do the job in this country, we will become a banana republic. I do not know if the government realizes that. By cutting education and cutting money to students for education, what the government is doing is bringing about a situa-
June 10, 1991

tion in which we are going to have a lot of people under-trained, under-educated and under-skilled and we will become a country with a much smaller capacity to produce and to cut that deficit.
If you really want to cut the deficit, you invest in things which will make you more productive. To quote the president of the Canadian Federation of Students: "Students represent Canada's single most important investment in the future. Human resources are the source of our greatest productivity in this century and at this time. It is absolute nonsense to cut programs that will help people contribute to the economy of this country and that is what you are doing when you squelch on your youth, your education and your employment programs."
There is a lot that could be said in this debate. For example, apprentices, because they lack hope, are dropping out of apprenticeship programs. I have here a special article from Statistics Canada pointing out that over 40 per cent of the 50,000 participants in apprenticeship programs drop out because they feel they have no hope of getting a job when their apprenticeship program is over. That is just another example.
The government's policy in this matter is cock-eyed. It says it is committed to the training of youth, to the education of youth and to the employment of youth, but that is rhetoric. The facts speak for themselves. The government says one thing but it does another. I say to the government: "Wake up. You are ruining the country and the country's future. Change your policies now before it is too late. If you want to ask us what should be done, we will tell you to do more of what was done in the last four or five years and you would be doing something."
Mr. Garth T\irner (Halton-Peel): Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a comment or two to the hon. member because he stood in his place and threw around a bunch of numbers about unemployment and also gave this House the distinct impression that the government has abandoned young Canada and is doing nothing.
I just want to remind the member that problems of youth unemployment are not new. As the member should well know, when he was part of the previous government and we can hearken back to the last reces-
Supply
sion, there was a youth unemployment rate of almost 18 per cent in 1982 in the month of May. In 1983 there was over 20 per cent unemployment among youth.
Now that compares with May of last year at around 12 per cent and May of this year at 16 per cent, which is still too high. I think we will all admit that, but the hon. member has an obligation to put this into a context that means something, instead of just giving us a lot of rhetoric.
On the issue of this government having abandoned youth, I think the member and the House need to be reminded, and the statement should be corrected by saying that in February of last year the government announced a program worth almost $300 million just aimed specifically at this problem. That is not all. Summer Employment Experience Development Program is in place now for $80 million; work orientation workshops, $35 million; student business loans almost $1 million; Canada Employment Centre for students almost $10 million. This is serious money that is being spent.
I have one question for the member and it centres around one comment he made. He said there was a ridiculous argument that the government is cutting back on expenditures because we have a debt. I want to ask the member if he realizes that nothing hurts our youth more than debt. If we have cuts today it is because we had debts yesterday and the chickens are coming home to roost. We are poisoning the future and, what is most important, our youth knows it.
I would like to ask the member to rise in his place and tell us if he is going to accept and acknowledge his responsibility as a parliamentarian to stop squandering the future of this country.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the member for giving me that question. Of course we have to cut the debt, but you do not cut the debt by cutting back on education; you do not cut back the debt by cutting back on training; you do not cut back the debt by cutting research and development. If you are really interested in cutting the debt, you increase the productivity of the country. You increase the climate in which people will invest and they will find trained and skilled people in this country. The last thing you cut is education and pro-

June 10,1991
grams relating to education, including summer employment programs for students. Yes, you cut, but you do not cut in those areas which will hinder your ability to produce more. The way you cut back on the deficit is by becoming a country with fewer unemployed and greater productivity.
That is my answer to that question.
With respect to the other question, he referred to 1981-82. We had a serious recession in 1981-82 and there was a high rate of unemployment, but the Liberal government of the day increased its spending for summer employment, increased its training programs and increased its programs for students; it kept people in university. Look at the record.
We increased the programs. I was part of the government. 1 was in Parliament. We increased the spending because we thought it was important to prime the pump and put people back to work.
What does this government do? It cuts. It cut by 35 per cent in 1990. It increased by a measly 2.5 per cent this year.
In answer to the hon. member, this is not the Liberals speaking. This is not the New Democrats speaking. I will refer to the president of the Canadian Federation of Students who says, and I quote from a press release of February 4, 1991, after the Challenge program was announced: "This government's record on student employment programs is appalling". I will spell it: a-p-p-a-1-1-i-n-g, appalling. That is the Canadian Federation of Students, not the Liberal Party.
Hear. hear.

Mr. Speaker, I want to speak today on this particular motion and to assure my hon. colleague that this government is committed to the youth of Canada and to youth employment. We all want young Canadians to have every opportunity possible to take their part in the nation's economy. We do not want them sitting back watching it go by. We want Canadians and Canadian youth to be involved in this economy. That is why this government has invested millions of dollars every year on services and programs for the youth of Canada. Even in this time of budget restraint we recognize that these kinds of programs must take place.
I want to point out to my colleague that the motion he has placed before the House completely ignores the reality of the situation. This motion only confirms that my hon. colleague shows a disturbing insensitivity to the real issues of youth employment. Youth employment is not simply providing a make-work project here or a make-work project there, a simple task of creating a few more jobs. The real key is the same one that affects employment for Canadians as a whole. That key is to develop our education and our training systems so that we can meet the challenges that face us in a global economy.
We must recognize that because our economic health as a country, which is our ability to compete, depends on how well we prepare young Canadians to take their places in the work force of tomorrow. We cannot afford to ignore the needs of our young Canadians, and we are not.
Since this government came to office there has been considerable progress made on behalf of the young people in this country. Millions of dollars have been committed to youth initiatives particularly in my area, certainly in southern Ontario and in the greater Toronto area where there are many competing demands for very limited resources.
We are meeting this challenge and we will continue to do so. Thousands of young Canadians use our programs to access skills, training and jobs. That includes all members of society. Right now hundreds of students are heading into the summer job market in my area and I can assure the hon. member that we are well aware that this is one of the toughest summers in which to land a job.
It being two o'clock p.m., the House will now proceed to Statements by Members pursuant to Standing Order 31.

Mr. Speaker, several hundred people in the seasonal clam fishery in my riding have found themselves unable to earn a living because there is no market for their product.
June 10, 1991

The people involved reside along the Five Islands- Economy Shore and have no other means of support. Their situation has come as a surprise and caught them off guard. Their problems are compounded because their unemployment insurance benefits have now run out.
Through no fault of their own, hundreds of people have no source of income to feed their families. I ask that the Department of Employment and Immigration extend their UIC benefits for the few weeks required until the fishery market is re-established.
Although there are several programs to help Atlantic Canadian fishermen, these people seem to have fallen through the cracks. Part of the problem is an overabundance of American product which should be depleted shortly and allow the Canadian product to find a market.
I appreciate that departmental officials and the minister have all been very supportive. I urge them to find a solution to this problem as quickly as they can.

Mr. Speaker, whatever the other results, I believe that all ministers and all members of the House will agree that the inquiry into the Al-Mashat affair has seriously damaged the anonymity and impartiality of the Public Service.
The delicate relationship of accountability and mutual trust must exist between the elected and the appointed servants of the Canadian public.
The Public Service of Canada is the most important instrument we have as parliamentarians to ensure that the programs and policies determined by this House are determined impartially, efficiently and effectively, and to ensure that the government and Parliament are well informed and advised in determining the future of the nation.
In order to begin to repair the damage, I urge the Prime Minister personally to take responsibility for establishing a special committee of this House to examine and report to Parliament on restoring the proper balance of accountability, responsibility, anonymity and impartiality in the relationship between the elected and appointed servants of Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I want to show you the youth situation, according to the labour market analysis made by the Canada Employment Center for Val-d'Or and Senneterre.
As you know, young people must face numerous difficulties on the labour market, the unemployment level being very high.
Moreover, jobs available are very often at entrance level in the hospitality or restaurant business or in retail sales. The working conditions are less competitive in these sectors and there is a high turnover.
It is no surprise then that young recipients give as their main occupation handling, administration, sales or services. The education level of young people in the labour market is high enough for the kind of work available.
However, the moment there is job specialization, young people have integration problems. I must mention that the drop-out phenomenon is reaching young people in our area too.
Mr. Speaker, life is not easy for today's youth, but it is encouraging to note that, since 1984, it is getting better. Only through our continued combined efforts will we get the best results.

Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George-Bulkley
Valley): Mr. Speaker, next year is Canada's 125th birthday. Canadians from coast to coast to coast will be celebrating a country that recently has had a difficult time.
Especially for aboriginal people, 1992 takes on a different meaning. At the New Democrats convention in Halifax this weekend we recognized this fact and have urged all Canadians and their governments to ensure that a serious message about aboriginal people is considered in any plans for 1992.
The recent shift of Canada 125 from the Secretary of State for External Affairs to the Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs is a sign that hopefully the government will consider all regions of the country when planning its events.

June 10, 1991
We want to ensure that when we celebrate 1992 all parts of the country can participate, and not just Ottawa. Only through a grassroots celebration across Canada will we achieve the true national unity we are all striving for.

Mr. Speaker, this House of Commons is devoting many hours today to a debate on the plight of our young people.
Opposition members are suggesting that the government solve the problem of youth unemployment by spending more money, money it does not possess and would have to be borrowed.
This is not what young people want. Instead, they want us to stop mortgaging their future with more debt.
As Jonathan Will writes from British Columbia: "No one in this country has more at stake in our current struggle with the escalating national debt than young Canadians".
As a young Canadian himself Mr. Will is asking us, the parliamentarians of this country, to stem the tide of red ink. Young Canada wants us to cut spending and free the future, not to borrow further and squander that birthright.
We have a responsibility in this House to do exactly that. The future does not belong to this generation and it is time we gave it back.

Mr. Speaker, you may be interested to know that Quebec's Minister of the Environment, Pierre Paradis, has urged the federal government to play a stronger role in the environmental assessment of the impact of the James Bay II project. We can only hope that the federal Minister of the Environment heard this unprecedented call for help.
Rafferty-Alameda, Oldman Dam and Kemano II are dam construction projects where the federal government had to be taken to court before it would respect its own environmental impact assessment laws.
The James Bay II project runs the risk of being added to this list of court defeats if the government does not live up to its environmental responsibilities.
Will the new Minister of the Environment listen to his Quebec colleague and do the right thing? We hope so.

Mr. Speaker, school holidays will start soon and I would like to offer my best wishes to all students for an excellent summer and a well-deserved rest. In my riding, I attended some events at the secondary, college and university levels designed to recognize the exceptional talents of our students. I have no doubt that those young Canadians will assert themselves and take their rightful place in our society.
I also want to take this opportunity to tell those students who are thinking of dropping out to immediately discuss their plans with their parents, teachers ou principals. If they make known their intentions, they will get to discover the different solutions that we, as a government, offer them and they will find that people are willing to help them evaluate the effects of such a decision.

Mr. Speaker, a short time ago my provincial counterpart, Mr. Neil Gaudry, and I visited the St. Boniface Hospital Research Centre to examine the Magnetic Resonance Imaging Scanner. This machine which performs critical diagnostic and research functions puts St. Boniface Hospital in the forefront of medical research in my native province, indeed in all of Canada.
There is an important message here. If Manitobans were not continually ravaged by, for example, the loss of the CF-18 contract, massive cuts to health and education, the closing of the Portage la Prairie military base, what about Shilo, the decimation of Manitoba's trucking
June 10, 1991

industry, the reduction of CN workers' complement by over 20 per cent, the possible rerouting of CP Rail's trains through the U.S., the almost total annihilation of VIA Rail, the privatization of Air Canada resulting in loss of jobs and the virtual gutting of CBC, what would happen? Where will it stop?
The message is very simple. We would thrive. Give us the support we need and deserve and we will hold our own. In fact we will excel at it.

Mr. Speaker, the membership of the Royal Canadian Legion believes in a united Canada and has since the organization's inception in 1925. It recognizes the need for change in our political structure, in the bureaucracy and in the Constitution. It believes through compromise and understanding Canadians working together can and will overcome these obstacles.
The Royal Canadian Legion supports: (1) a strong and united Canada, (2) a guarantee of individual rights and freedoms, (3) a policy of two official languages at the national level, (4) a need for a political framework supporting our continued existence as a nation, and (5) a simplified process to amend the Constitution.
Canadian unity is being threatened by separatists not only in Quebec but in western Canada. They want to divide our country. I urge Canadians to tell the likes of Parizeau, Bouchard and Manning that we believe in a United Canada. We are proud to be Canadians.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week we learned that a firm named Multinational Resources, listed on the Vancouver Stock Exchange and with strong links with U.S. companies, announced its intention to dam the North Thompson River, which is a tributary of the Fraser River at Vavenby, British Columbia, in order to divert water into the Columbia River basin which
would eventually be delivered to the San Diego, California market.
This is occurring which the federal government begins negotiations to conclude a free trade agreement with Mexico and the United States.
We are aware that the governor of California, last month, indicated that he was anxious in purchasing fresh water from Canada for his state. We are reminded that the North America Water and Power Alliance proposal calls for British Columbia and Yukon Rivers to be damned and diverted into the United States and northern Mexico. We also know that the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement did not say that Canada's rivers would not be diverted to flow into the United States.
I call upon the government to speak up and say that Canada's rivers will not be sold to the United States; that our fresh water is just that, our fresh water; that Canadians will not allow our rivers to be diverted wholly or partially to be sold in the United States or northern Mexico.

Mr. Speaker, Quebec Premier Bourassa says that a constituent assembly is an uncalculated risk that is not worth taking.
Last year the premier took a calculated risk on 11 middle aged white men in blue suits meeting behind closed doors. He says he will not do that again. He is prepared to risk negotiating but only with the federal government. That is a risk, however, that English speaking Canadians find totally unacceptable because both the Prime Minister and the premier come from Quebec.
A constituent assembly may be an uncalculated risk, but it is a risk that 68 per cent of Canadians outside Quebec and 57 per cent of Canadians in Quebec say they want to take. That makes it the only risk that is acceptable to a majority of Canadians.
Surely, if we learned nothing else from Meech Lake, we learned that it is not worth taking the risk if it is not acceptable to the majority of Canadians.

June 10,1991

Mr. Speaker, when the hated goods and services tax went into effect on January 1, books started to be taxed in Canada for the first time since Confederation.
Back in November the Prime Minister said that he would reconsider the tax on books if there was proof the industry was being adversely affected, that is the book business.
Now there is proof, proof not only that book businesses are being adversely affected but also that education is suffering.
Canadian book publishers' sales dropped by 12 per cent since the tax was introduced. However, the more worrisome figures are these: sales of books to Canadian colleges and universities were down 23 per cent for the first quarter of this year and net sales to schools were down 34 per cent in March.
Can this be passed off as just another effect of the recession? No, Mr. Speaker, because during the 1980-83 recession Canadian book sales actually increased by nearly 54 per cent.
There are other troubling wrinkles that have resulted from the tax on books, a tax that sets Canada apart. Many foreign publishers, particularly smaller ones and those whose books are not taxed in their home countries, are so aghast at having to file monthly tax returns to the Canadian government that they decided not to bother shipping to Canada.
In March, the government lifted the GST from human sperm donated for artificial insemination. Surely books and the education of Canada's younger generation are important enough to be added to that list.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Youth); Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)

Mr. Speaker, on May 31, I was invited to visit a food business in my riding called La come d'abondance, formerly Le verger naturel.
This business, which is owned by two young people who succeeded their father after he had spent many years running it, many years is a striking example of a
takeover by young dynamic people who are sensitive to the present needs of their customers.
Mr. Speaker, I was enthusiastic and impressed by the cleanliness, the concern for the environment, and the emphasis on product packaging and quality.
I am convinced that those young people will succeed in making this business what we could call an example for other youths who have the desire to carve out a niche in our active society.

Mr. Speaker, in Halifax at the NDP Convention, the delegates passed a resolution to move us closer to a constituent assembly in this country.
Also over the weekend the Conservative premier of Nova Scotia, Premier Cameron, endorsed the idea of a constituent assembly on the Constitution. That now brings it to five premiers in the country who endorse the idea: Premier Cameron in Nova Scotia; Premier McKenna of New Brunswick; Premier Wells, the Liberal premier in Newfoundland; Premier Rae in Ontario; and Premier Devine in Saskatchewan.
In light of the growing momentum, as Premier Wells says on this particular issue, I would urge the Canadian government across the way to consider the possibility of a constituent assembly as a means of opening up the process and making it really accessible and democratic for all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, one of Canada's best kept secrets last month was the outstanding success of the Prime Minister's visit to Japan in promoting new dimensions of trade and diplomatic relations with that country.
As one who was privileged to be invited as a member of the Canadian delegation, I can speak first hand and proudly of the impressive performance by the Prime Minister in addressing the profound potential for trade in goods and services and for two-way investment which exists between Canada and Japan.
June 10, 1991

The Prime Minister's message was clear and simple: Canada is keen to increase its business with Japan in both directions. There is much to offer for each country: large markets, good products, innovative services, and a political and economic climate which is stable and compatible.
The Japanese response was equally straightforward. Their citizens admire and respect Canada. That respect was best expressed by the full participation of Japan's leaders at the opening of the new Canadian Embassy on May 27, an event to make any Canadian extremely proud.
It is too bad more news has not been made in Canada of this successful trip.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Acting Prime Minister.
Four years ago next week the former Minister of Finance unveiled a tax package in which he claimed that future tax changes like the GST were going to be "revenue neutral" and that in fact "most Canadians will pay lower taxes". That is what the minister said on June 18, 1987.
Yesterday, his successor finally admitted what Canadians had known for months, and that is that Canadians under this government's policies are taxed to the limit and they will not take it any more.
Oral Questions
In fact the Tory tax machine is so voracious that the GST has raised 18 per cent more than predicted: $400 million, to be precise.
I ask the Acting Prime Minister: When will his government announce an 18 per cent cut in the GST rate to give Canadian taxpayers a break at the very least, or when will he end this vicious GST?

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the minister for industry and international trade. There were 15,000 more people unemployed in the month of May. Full-time jobs have fallen by 330,000 since this time last year, and the most recent economic report from the Bank of Montreal says that the recovery is going to be weak and sluggish. Will this government take Canada out of the free trade deal and give us back our economic independence?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think the hon. member is telling anybody on this side of the House that people are hurting. We understand that and it is something about
which other ministers and myself have expressed a good deal of concern.
For the hon. member to say that we should get out of the free trade agreement tells me that the hon. member is not understanding the impact of the free trade agreement on the economy. There is no question we have been in recession, but if we had not had the free trade agreement we would have been in a deeper recession because the trade surplus with the United States has gone from $14 billion in 1988 to $17 billion in
1990.	Our exports to the United States have increased by 12 per cent during that period, and we have seen a net change in the net flow of foreign direct investment into Canada, a change in the net positive basis for Canada, of $6 billion. All of those have created jobs in this country and have ensured that the recession is not more serious in its impact.

Mr. Speaker, the minister likes to talk about the trade surplus. Let us talk about the whole current account balance because the fact is Canada had a current account surplus with the United States in 1988 and since the trade deal we have had a deficit of over $3 billion. That means lost jobs.
Is this minister prepared to start to do something about the whole host of problems with this trade deal, the fact that our energy policy moves are blocked, the fact that we are not able to make the moves to give Canadian content in our various industries, all those things that are stopping new jobs from being established in this country? Will this minister in fact give us back our independence as a nation?
