Madam Speaker, as I was saying before-we were interrupted an hour and a half ago-right now this is a very difficult time for students heading into the summer job market. Most of us are cognizant of that fact.
I for one am very pleased with the government's response in trying to assist these students and help them into the job market.
We are making the best use of the resources we have at hand. Right now in Canada we have about 400 Canada Employment Centres that last year provided opportunities for about 270,000 workers. In my particular area we have about 17 employment centres and last year they provided approximately 11,000 high school, college and university students the opportunity to get jobs in their particular areas. One thing that is very important is the Canada Employment Centres are working very, very hard.
One of the things they are doing is helping kids to beat the odds when it comes to employment by teaching them how to look for work. Today, it is not a question of
banging on doors, asking for jobs, and the doors opening. It takes a more sophisticated approach. We are teaching our students and young people how to prepare themselves for a job interview and how to prepare a good resume.
I think that is very important to them not only for this summer but for the future when they are applying for more permanent jobs at different other times in their lives.
Canada Employment Centres are only part of the bigger picture. I think that is one of the things we should be talking about today because thousands of post-secondary students across Canada have found summer jobs through COSEP. In fact this year already in my particular area there have been over 900 students who have already found jobs under this program. In Ontario alone this year, under Challenge '91 over $18 million is going to be spent on employment programs for students including SEED, the kind of program that is going to help students not only this year but in the future. These programs- and last year just in Ontario alone there were over 9,500 of them-help students get experience in a job market they are often related to or interested in.
I think that is very important because we have increased our resources in Ontario for this co-op education under the Canadian Jobs Strategy Program. That is a very popular program and without it many Canadians would not be able to finish their university education. When you look at those kinds of numbers and those types of programs, that is very important to the youth of our nation.
The question of summer jobs, as I mentioned, is only one concern of this government's youth initiatives. Our interest in youth employment goes well beyond how many jobs are available this summer. That is the simplistic answer, and that is the simplistic part of it.
We are focusing on meeting the long-term needs of many young Canadians, those who need help the most. In the 1990s job market, those youths are facing a lifetime of employment problems, not just this summer.
When we look at the programs offered by Employment and Immigration Canada, we see that it is going to play a major role in ensuring that these young people get the employment skills, the education and the training that they need. Programs like Job Entry are working very
June 10, 1991

successfully to give this group the employment skills that they need.
In metropolitan Toronto, there is more than $6 million being employed in the Canadian Jobs Strategy to help unemployed youth. This program targets those who have left school and who are trying to enter a very tight labour market, frankly, with very few if any training skills, marketable skills and the things that are necessary to land and keep a job.
Under the job entry program, these young people will gain employment skills and classroom training aimed at long-term employment.
I was at one of these centres not too long ago. These centres are providing youth with assistance, providing them with the ability to choose the type of career that they might be interested in, and providing an opportunity for them to get into a career. Those kinds of programs are working very well.
That is a co-operative type of program between the private sector, government, institutions and municipalities. Those are very substantive programs, and I think they help an awful lot.
Some of the things that we are doing for our youth are also directed to those young people, those Canadians who have simply run out of options.
One of the difficulties when you look at Canadian youth today-you often see them, Madam Speaker, when you visit our larger metropolitan centres from coast to coast to coast-is that there are children who are just lost in the system. They are not able to find their position in society.
When we look at the different backgrounds, whether they come from a broken home or from a ghetto-type of society which is poverty based, I think that we have to really consider and address the future that these children have.
When you combine that poverty factor and the low educational factor of these children who have dropped out of school, we are really looking at a very serious difficulty, and not just for the immediate short term but in the long run.
These Canadians are on the margin of society with no way to get back into society. They want to be contributing members, but frankly there are not a lot of people who want to take a chance on these young children.
Supply
I firmly believe that the actions and the activities that this government is taking are really going to help this generation and this group of people. I know that the Minister of State for Youth is very dedicated and very committed to this particular mission.
There are a number of programs right now in the metropolitan area which I represent that are going on for these youths who are severely employment disadvantaged. Many of these projects will provide the kind of assistance that will help these young people get better employment and better training.
If we can do that, it does an awful lot of other things for these children, because it gives them an outlook on life. It gives them a future. It gives them something to look forward to.
I know that the Metro-Youth Job Corps is one of their programs. It seems to work very well and it has been very efficient. It is not focused on short-term benefits. These children who are involved in it are getting a chance to learn generic job skills, valuable life skills that will help them to help themselves.
If we can do that, we are doing the kind of work that is really necessary for a government. If we can instil that sense of accomplishment, that sense of success in these young people, then they will go on and have a sense of purpose and a goal in their life. If we can do that, I think we will have been very successful.
Up until now, of the young people who take part in these programs, about 70 per cent go on to find permanent employment. These are young people who have had very difficult times in their backgrounds. It is really great to see that kind of result coming out of those kinds of programs.
There is another program. That is work done by the Kensington Youth Theatre ensemble, which one would think would not have too much to do with youth employment. However, if you look at the program, they learn how to be carpenters, how to be plumbers, learn other kinds of skills, writing skills, and team building. Those are the kinds of opportunities that our young Canadians are looking for.
The other thing this government is doing very substantively is encouraging Toronto kids and Ontario kids and Canadian kids to stay in school. One of the things that is very disturbing, I think, to all Canadians, particularly those in government, is the fact that 30 per cent of our

June 10, 1991
Supply
youth are dropping out of high school before they finish their high school education.
That is roughly about the same number that goes on to finish university education. I do not think that is a very good ratio. That is something that is really heartbreaking and it is a loss of human potential for Canadian society. We just cannot afford to let those numbers continue. We have to get these children back into school to get the education required to be better citizens of Canada.
That is why I support the stay-in-school initiative. It is something this government is doing to tackle this problem and to not accept this totally unacceptably high dropout rate. This stay-in-school initiative is intended to encourage young people to stay in school and complete their education so that they will be better equipped to enter a highly competitive labour market.
Looking at these kinds of programs, such as the work orientation workshops under Challenge 91-another program to help those children who have recently dropped out of school and are now at risk because of the fact that they do not have that graduation certificate- this powerful combination is an effective technique for providing recent and potential dropouts with new options. By providing them with practical work experience related to their career choices, young people are learning the skills to become productive members of Canada's labour force.
This program also gives our youth a realistic picture of the world at work. I can assure this House that a glimpse of life at the minimum wage of $5 is not going to be too exciting to a high school dropout when they realize that by staying in school, they can get a much better, much more productive and much more rewarding job.
We estimate that we are looking at about 30 projects under the work orientation workshop in Ontario. I think that speaks for itself. Over 400 students will be able to take part in this program.
Our youth programs reflect our national commitment to ensure that Canadians continue to enjoy the benefits of a globally competitive economy. However, our prosperity depends on improving our ability to compete and improving the levels of skills held by all Canadians.
Canadians are now becoming more aware of the extent of the employment challenges facing all of us. One of
the factors is that fewer young people are entering the labour force, compared to the baby boom years, and they just do not have the training and skills needed for some of the jobs that are available today.
That means that our young Canadians will not be able to provide all of the new skills that the economy demands. New skills requirements will also have to be met by retraining people who are already in the work force.
Canada's youth will continue to be an important part of the learning culture we are building, but it is a lengthy and a complex process in a country as diverse as ours. By working with young Canadians, we are already pursuing one of the most important first steps in this process.
I am confident that the youth programs this government has followed will provide a foundation for a strong and very competitive Canada.

Madam Speaker, first of all I would like to say that the member for York-Simcoe, who has just finished giving a very passionate address, knows of the respect in which I hold him.
However, I want to make a couple of comments and ask a specific question. First of all, I certainly agree that the Government of Canada is trying to teach our youth how to take a much more sophisticated approach to looking for a job. He talked about a career oriented approach. He talked about the preparation of good resumes. He talked about all of the things that would hopefully make looking for the desired work a more satisfying experience.
Does the hon. member not realize that even with the best skills and the most sophisticated resume-and he knows from his own riding and certainly the greater Toronto area-that the $6 million for the metropolitan area really only works out to about $15 per student who is looking for a job right now.
Second, does he not realize that the problem is not with our youth who have the sophistication, the work ethic and who want to go out and do something constructive rather than sit at home for the summer? Does he not realize, and I am sure he does, that the real problem right now is that our housing industry has basically been frozen in the province of Ontario, especially in his own
June 10,1991

region? Does he not realize that, because of problems we are having-not just the GST but other costs in general-that our tourism, food services and hospitality industry has basically shut down? When many of these youths apply for jobs this year, there is just nothing there. There are no jobs right now for carpenters. There are no jobs for plumbers. There are no jobs for youths who drive trucks, dump trucks or whatever.
My question is, what do we say to those youths who go door to door, business after business? It does not matter whether it is a restaurant or a construction site or a lodge in northern Ontario or whatever. What do we say to those sophisticated youths who are right now getting shut out everywhere they go?
He must realize that the problem is not with our youth. The problem is that we have to figure out a way, in short order, to get confidence back in our small and medium-sized business community, which represents 80 per cent of the jobs, especially in our province. We have to get that industry fired up so that it in turn will have the confidence to meet that payroll, which in turn will give those youths a job. What does he say to those youths who are getting shut out everywhere they go right now in spite of many good government programs?

Madam Speaker, I want to thank the member for Broadview-Greenwood for his comments and his questions.
One of the things about the member for Broadview- Greenwood that I have always been impressed with is that he is often willing to provide suggestions and alternatives. I think that is a constructive type of opposition and a constructive type of government, which we should be looking at more and more often. I really respect the member for that.
He mentioned a couple of things I want to comment on. One was the limited number of dollars the federal government is spending. The member opposite knows the problem of budget restraints and knows the problem of the deficit and the debt we are facing. I do not think the youth of our country want us to say: "Here is a handout for a job here. Here is a handout for a job there. It is going to look after you for the next couple of
Supply
months, but you are going to pay for it for the rest of your life". I think the hon. member could agree with me on that.
I do not think those kinds of programs are what is necessary. I think it is important, and I agree with him that it is not a problem with our youth. Our youth of today want to get jobs. They want to work and they want to contribute. I think he is quite correct that there is a malaise in the small business community, particularly in Ontario. In fact there is a frustration in the small business community right now. One of the things they are finding difficult is a provincial government that is really harnessing in on them. It is not giving them any opportunities to be productive. It is not giving them any opportunities for new employment, for new construction, for some of the things that we have talked about. Because of some of the things it is doing, there is no incentive for that land owner to build an apartment building and hire a bunch of students for the summer who could do some of the plumbing and some of the roughing in work and this kind of thing.
Fortunately, in our area, the construction industry does seem to be starting to come around now, but it is a very slow process and these small business owners who are involved in this kind of thing are very, very frustrated. They cannot even decide whether they are going to work Monday to Friday or Tuesday to Saturday or just what it is going to be. They are passing that buck back.
The small business owner today in Ontario is facing a lot of burdens with increased taxes and a deficit that they do not know where it is going. It is very difficult for that small business owner. But I hope that the small business owner is going to be able to see his way through and provide some of these jobs. I know that one of the things youth will do is take a chance. They are willing to say: "Hey, I will work a little extra hard this week or today and work for a little less because I want to make a success of it." I know our Canadian youth will make a success of it.

Madam Speaker, I listened with interest to my hon. friend who suggests that the small business community is having a difficult time in the province of Ontario.

June 10, 1991
Supply
I want to tell him that the small business community is having a difficult time beyond Ontario and in British Columbia things are not very encouraging. They are not very encouraging in Saskatchewan, Alberta, Quebec and Atlantic Canada. So I do not think we want to focus in fact by suggesting that in one province things are significantly different.
But I do want to ask my friend a question. For this year's Challenge '91 program, I must have had 300 or 400 or even more small businesses who wanted to participate in the program. Some staff people had to phone about 240 of those small businesses and say: "I am sorry, there is nothing we can do for you." They wanted to hire a student or sometimes two or three students, but literally, for all intents and purposes, almost all of those small businesses had to be phoned and just told: "Listen, there is no funding. We cannot include you in this student employment program for the summer."
My question is to my hon. friend. I know he is a sincere individual and it is not a critical comment that I am levelling at him, but would he not think it would be a good investment, in terms of investing in Canada's most important natural resource, to say to small businesses that if you are interested it will make a difference for you to hire a student this summer, we would like to participate with you? Would he not think that would be a good way to invest taxpayers' money?

Madam Speaker, I thank the hon. member for his question.
The reason I was referring to Ontario in my previous answer was the fact that that was how the question was directed to me and I thought it was best to respond to the question. It is one of the things I try to do. I know a lot of members have difficulty with that at times, but I was trying to relate to the question as it was asked. I was not referring or suggesting that it was going to be easier in any other part of the country.
But I do want to recognize the member's question. He said that the government is not taking part. I think the member also knows that the federal government put $80 million into the SEED program this year in co-operation with small business to help create summer jobs. I think $35 million was put into the WILD program.
So you have to look at that kind of thing and you can separate and pick out one part of it or another part of the program or the different programs and say: "Well this
program was reduced". I am not going to suggest to the member that it was not reduced, but there are other programs that have been increased at the same time.
I think it is only fair that you look at the over-all budget and at the over-all programming. I think the efforts by the government to provide this kind of encouragement to our youth is very, very positive.

Madam Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43(2) I would like to share my speaking slot with my hon. friend from Prince George-Bulkley Valley.
First of all, let me begin by indicating what we are actually doing here today. We are responding to an opposition motion that this House call upon the government to implement immediate measures to alleviate the devastatingly high rate of unemployment amongst Canadian youth.
In other words, we are appealing to the government to do something about a situation that I suspect many people would consider to be immoral, to be completely unacceptable, to be wrong. We are saying to the federal government that as we look out across the Canadian landscape there are thousands, tens of thousands, hundreds of thousands of young people who do not have a job in one of the wealthiest countries of the world. For that to occur we should be considering that to be not only unacceptable but immoral. What we are saying is that we are abandoning those young people. We are saying to those tens of thousands of young people "watch television or whatever, sit around and chit-chat with your pals; we are not interested in you participating in Canadian society in a meaningful way and participating in the building of the country". That is what we are saying, Madam Speaker.
But let me be more specific; that is what the government is saying, because as we have heard there are all sorts of proposals, all sorts of ideas from a number of speakers in the opposition. I think it is time that we acknowledged the fact that the most important natural resource in this country is not codfish, oil, gas, coal, wheat or trees; it is the people of Canada and particularly the young people of Canada. We should be investing in that natural resource, developing that natural resource, encouraging and nurturing that natural resource, like we have never done before.
June 10, 1991

What are we doing? Virtually nothing. I know the government will say "we have this ZIP program and SEED program and ZET program, and so on". But that is not even touching the surface of the problem, it is not beginning to resolve youth unemployment this summer. I have two sons, one going to university and one finishing high school. They are out trying to find summer jobs. There are all kinds of jobs that they can line up for, but they apply and there are 200 other young people applying for that same single job. It pays $5.50 an hour. They have to raise funds to continue their studies at universities, colleges and technical schools, and so on. Their friends are the same.
It is very frustrating for these young people to ask: do people not care? Does this country not care about us? Does the government not care about us?
That is why I put the question to one of my colleagues on the government bench. I know in my own constituency of Kamloops, when it came to the Challenge '91 program, we had applications from businesses, large and small, applications from non-profit societies, applications from municipalities and regional districts and hospitals and colleges that wanted to participate in what they thought was a government program to hire young people. They were prepared to put up good money and have the federal government match it, or in some cases ask the federal government to provide the meaningful job for a young person in an art gallery or in a municipality in an activity of one kind or another.
We had to reject almost all of the applications because we did not have enough money. We probably could only meet probably 20 per cent of the applications, and that is a business that would ask for three positions. "We can employ three young people", and they get one. Or a non-profit organization is prepared to hire seven young people to run a nursery program for single parents and we could maybe find two people for that particular group.
So there are all kinds of jobs out there. I think it is about time that the federal government says it wants to participate, in most cases with the provincial jurisdiction, and provide those meaningful summer jobs so that young people can go out and work in the summer and permit
Supply
them then to return to school and their studies in the fall, having participated in a few weeks of work, to say nothing of part-time work, or to say nothing of all of those tens of thousands of young people who are simply unemployed, who have less schooling for a variety of reasons. Perhaps they have even graduated from secondary school or graduated from college and simply cannot find a job.
As we saw earlier, Madam Speaker, that is resulting in 16 per cent of young people between the ages of 15 and 25 who want to work and cannot work. There are no jobs. It is 16 per cent. I will tell you that there are many countries in the world that would not tolerate that. They would consider that to be the basis of a crisis that had to be addressed.
I remember something that occurred in Sweden not too many years ago. As you know, Madam Speaker, Sweden has practised many of the traditions of social democracy no matter what government has been in place, essentially that mentality continues on.
They looked out and saw what was happening in their country. They saw to their astonishment that 11 per cent of Swedish young people were unemployed. The Conservative government of the day in that country said: "This is wrong. This ought not to be. There ought not to be any young people out of work."
It said: "Within three years, we want to implement programs to ensure that every single one of those young Swedish men and women are meaningfully employed or involved in training or education programs of one kind or another." It set out to do that.
It created programs to encourage small businesses to hire young people on training programs. It encouraged young people through increased bursaries and scholarships to attend technical, vocational schools, colleges and universities. It set out a whole series of private initiated programs to help young mothers, single parents and seniors to go into the forests and practise silviculture methods. They went in and stabilized the banks of all sorts of mountain streams and so on to halt erosion. There were all sorts of programs that actually work to make Sweden a better place.

June 10, 1991
Supply
Do you know what happened, Madam Speaker? Yes, it required the government paying a bit more but it was already paying those young people some form of welfare or unemployment insurance. It topped those funds up and within three years every single one of those people were meaningfully employed and/or involved in society with their studies, or training or work programs. This includes every single one of them.
Then, those young people, as a result of the fact that they were being paid reasonably well for the job they were doing, they would purchase things. They bought Volvos. They bought clothes. They went out and entertained. They participated as regular citizens, and consequently, sales taxes flowed in, income taxes were paid along with excise taxes of various kinds.
In the end, the government virtually made money on that initiative. Not only was it cost effective in the long term after a three-year period, but every single young person in that country was meaningfully employed.
I realize that Sweden with eight million people cannot automatically transfer its experience to Canada, but we can certainly take the best portions of it and apply it where we can, whereas this government chooses to do virtually nothing which is an abandonment of the youth of this country.
I say that there are no shortages of examples in terms of what can be done. There are all kinds of proposals that we are hearing today.
We are begging the minister responsible for youth and, indeed, the government per se to begin to acknowledge the fact that the most important natural resource in this country are the people of Canada, particularly the young people of Canada. Right now, to ask them to go out and compete with the thousands and thousands of people who have lost their jobs and who have years of experience is not realistic.
We have only to find the comments made the other day by the Minister of State responsible for Finance and Privatization when he had the audacity to stand in this House and say: "There are lots of jobs for students. If they look hard for them, they will find them."
It is that attitude that obviously telegraphs that this minister and this government does not understand the
depth and seriousness of the problem. When he says: "If you really work hard, you will find a job," that is nonsense. It is wrong, and it is callous.
I do hope that the present Minister of Youth sees the world quite differently than the Minister of State responsible for Finance and Privatization and actually introduces quickly in the days and weeks ahead meaningful programs to ensure that businesses can hire young people for training programs and meaningful employment and that all sorts of other organizations can take advantage of the programs as well.

speakeroldname: Mr. Marcel R. TVemblay (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Minister of State (Youth) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Youth); Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in the course of this debate, one of my colleagues across the way said that the competitive position of Canadians was declining, and he quoted the report on world competitiveness.
I would like to point out, Madam Speaker, that Canada ranks fifth in the world on development of human resources. In 1990, it ranked third for the skills, motivation, flexibility and health of its population. In 1986, Canada ranked fourth, and in 1989, we ranked second.
I think the hon. member would agree that the ranking of third in the world is a vote of confidence by the international community in the quality of education, training and health of Canada's people, including youth. The recent Speech from the Throne makes it clear that the government is not resting on its laurels and will strive to improve Canada's performance in learning and to make the concept of lifelong learning a reality for all Canadians.
I have a question for the hon. member. The hon. member will agree that the private sector bears some responsibility for the creation of jobs, including summer jobs for students. Does the hon. member think that the federal government should subsidize summer jobs in Canada?
June 10, 1991

First of all, to answer the question specifically, obviously there is sharing between the private sector and government to ensure that young people find employment opportunities.
Let us recognize that the private sector is being beaten down these days. We know what is happening in terms of economic and financial statistics. We know what is happening to the business world, large and small. They are being pilloried. To expect them to be hiring the usual number of summer students is, I think, unrealistic. We have a list of many of the larger firms that are hiring for the summer, but for the small business persons these days it is almost impossible.
I say to my hon. friend that obviously there is a balance there, but the glowing statistics that my hon. colleague reads out about ranking fifth in the world for this or twenty-third in the world for that is not helping Mary Brown who is right now pounding the streets of this city looking for a summer job or little Jack Brown out there some place in Red Deer trying to find a job for the summer. It does not help these young people. It infuriates them to think that when there are programs that could be launched and when there are all sorts of initiatives that could be taken, the government is saying that we are ranking 13th in the world of this and we are doing well in terms of statistics. It demonstrates that it does not understand what is going on in the real world.
I encourage my hon. friend to get back to his constituency and talk to young people in the high schools and colleges and ask them how they are doing this summer. If his communities are like any other that I know in Canada, the young people are saying they are having a tough time. It is has been the toughest ever. The youth employment offices will be telling that in a formal way, if he does not want to go home and find that out. It is tough for students out there. It is very difficult for young people, and the government does not seem to be doing much about it.

Madam Speaker, I would just like to bring to the hon. member's attention to the fact that it is not just the private sector that needs to be motivated and encouraged. I realize that there are problems coast to coast in terms of youth unemployment, but I would like to be very specific.
In the province of Ontario we have a government that, granted it has been in power for only a year, has not approved one plan of subdivision, though there are close to 100,000 affordable housing unit projects on the books. Affordable shelter is something that we need, and this an area where literally 40,000 or 50,000 people could be employed overnight simply by the minister of housing
Supply
and the minister of municipal affairs putting a signature to plans of subdivision, as long as they concentrate on affordable shelter.
I would hope that the member uses his influence with his colleagues from the province to get the affordable shelter program moving.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George-Bulkley Valley):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I too want to thank the member for Kamloops for agreeing to share some of his time this afternoon in the short time we have to comment on the particular motion before the House today, an opposition motion and a very important one I think.
It is calling upon the government to implement immediate measures to alleviate the devastatingly high rate of unemployment among Canadian youth. I think I would certainly second the comments of the member for Kamloops when he talked about how important Canada's young people are. I stand in this House and talk a lot about our forests and our fish and our farms, but he is quite right: if anything is our most important resource in this country, it has to be Canada's people and, undoubtedly, Canada's young people as well.
I took the time today to listen to the member who led off the debate and to the minister to hear some of the comments that were said on this and the programs, of course, that are trotted out by the government.
It is fair to say that any of the members in their own ridings who work with the Canada Employment Centres on this area need an up-date about every other day to keep track of all the acronyms and the different programs that are there. Of course, one of the members acknowledged the fact that in a number of areas those programs have been cut back. In fact, we have also learned that a number of Student Employment Centres on campuses are going to be closed. They are closing 100 of them, including some at some fairly significant universities across the country: the University of Calgary, the University of New Brunswick and the Memorial University of Newfoundland.

June 10, 1991
Supply
As well, just before commenting a bit on the question of unemployment among young people, I do not think we could really talk about unemployment among young people unless we mentioned as well the impact that the GST is having on young people and the government's seemingly endless round of consultations on trying to change the Canada Student Loans Program.
It has shown up once again in the regulatory reform package, the book that comes out once a year. I am sure you go through that, Madam Speaker. It shows that once again the government is trying to study reforms to the Student Loans Program. It was a leftover from the previous year. We hope that for the first time in some time the Government of Canada will actually move on bringing the Canada Student Loans Program into the future so that we have a current program that works.
I took the opportunity during the break to actually have my staff call the two student centres in my riding in Prince George and Vanderhoof. I asked them to call to basically give me some information and advice that they might have about what is the current situation that students and young people are facing right now.
The comments from the Prince George Student Employment Centre are that the jobs are down this year and that they are primarily casual and odd jobs: lawn mowing, car washing and what have you.
Very importantly, and this is a comment I think I would like to add as well, in many of our rural communities it is very difficult often for young people to get employment. Often they rely on jobs to work in their mother or father's business or their mother or father's friend who has a business. One of example of that, a particular example, is in Vanderhoof where the Student Employment Centre there reports today that there is a dramatic drop in job listings, fewer jobs, but also a large increase in registrants. The comment made by the student employment officer there is that businesses are not hiring because they do not have the additional funds. Largely they are attributing that to the problems businesses are having in terms of reduced business from the GST. They
are deciding to go through the summer without doing that additional hiring.
As well, I had the opportunity a month or two ago where I thought it was important to go out and actually hear from young people to see exactly what the situation was. It was very interesting to hear from the presidents of student councils in the high schools in Prince George who actually commented that they felt, from talking to their constituents, that the number of jobs was done this summer.
We followed up after that meeting and the calls today again confirm exactly what they knew. They are likely better representatives than the government side, because they know what pressures are on their constituents and their fellow students. I would recommend to any member here who has not done that, to do it. If you cannot do it before the summer, meet this fall, as I am going to, with student council presidents so that you get a view and a sense from those young people as to exactly the situation they are facing.
It is clear, especially in a large number of rural communities, that young people are facing additional problems in finding employment in the larger centres, particularly in this case with the demands on young people these days in terms of seeing the messages on television about people travelling to Vancouver. There is real pressure on the smaller communities.
As members we participate in a number of projects. I tour a large number of the projects which are eventually funded, during the summer, to see how they are going and to find out how they are operating.
We face the same situation as the member for Kamloops. There is a vast number of employers, local governments, and non-profit organizations willing to participate and work with the federal government to employ young people, but this government obviously is not interested in that. There has slowly been the cutting back of these programs and making it ever more difficult for young people to get employment.
June 10, 1991

The throne speech, as I mentioned earlier today in comments to the minister, talks a great deal about education and training and how important they are. Coming from an area of B.C. where the participation rate in post-secondary education is very low, I welcome the initiative. I suppose it is the fifth or sixth time we have heard this initiative from the federal government about trying to get something going in this country on education and training. Let us hope it is successful this time. To date it has not been. I would certainly encourage any efforts in that particular area.
We are very pleased and honoured that in Prince George we will be getting the University of Northern B.C. shortly. The project is under way now. We hope it is not threatened by the ongoing cutbacks in funding from this government because of course that will play a major role in the whole question of employment in that area.
I want to close with one suggestion. The minister said he would be taking notes. He is not here now, but I know he is probably watching on television. In our ridings we have had the creation of our local advisory committees that provide advice to Canada Employment on various programs. Some of these work half decently and others struggle along. I would recommend to the minister that he consider a directive, if you like, or advice to those local advisory committees to ensure that there is representation from young people on those committees. They are often missed whenever a government or an institution starts talking about all the wonderful things it is going to do for young people. Of course the last group of people it ever consults or includes in the decision making is young people.
I just want to close with an appeal to the government to heed this motion. I hope it will support the motion. The fact is that something can be done.
Must be done.

"Must be done", says an hon. member. I agree with that. If this government can mobilize its intellectual, physical, mental and fiscal power such as it did when Canada participated in the gulf war, certainly there is no better cause in this country to mobilize the resources of the Canadian government than to help our young people.

Madam Speaker, I very much appreciated the member's intervention as it
Supply
relates to the pursuit of education and, in particular, the pursuit of excellence by way of post-secondary education.
I wonder if the member could comment on the recent ridiculous decision of the Ontario government to do away with recognition of the Ontario Student Awards Program, the single award that actually gave recognition to students at the secondary level for the pursuit of excellence.
If the hon. member does not agree with this decision, will he make his views known to the Government of Ontario?

Madam Speaker, I would be pleased to present any views to any government in Canada to improve education policy in this country, and in particular the Government of Ontario which is cleaning up after the mess left behind by the previous Liberal administration.
The tremendous challenge that faces Bob Rae and the New Democratic government of Ontario is to ensure that Ontario is on a competitive footing, to ensure that our education institutions in Ontario are funded to the highest level possible, and to deliver a message to this government, and we will do the same thing: "Stop cutting transfer payments to the provinces, do your job, improve funding to health and education in this country. It is desperately needed".

Madam Speaker, the government has recently established the Canadian Labour Force Development Board, which is an agency comprised of 22 members, representing a wide range of groups, such as business, labour, social groups and the educational community. It is a real partnership. I think it shows the commitment of the Government of Canada to get directly involved with the private sector and bring the private sector right into the job creation process. It is something I really want to applaud the government for doing.
I would like to ask the hon. member whether he thinks the establishment of this kind of board does not represent a fundamental and major step in improving the quality of Canada's education system? I wonder if he might comment on that because it strikes me that a partnership approach to finding solutions is the best way for us to go.

June 10, 1991
Supply

Madam Speaker, I appreciate the question from the member representing Halton-Peel. I know there has been some debate about this board. I think I could endorse some of the general principles behind it, but I would add a couple of additional comments.
All too often, I suppose, we have tended to emphasize a great deal the efforts here in Ottawa. I would certainly appeal to the government and the members of that board to reach out beyond the usual offices and bureaucracies of the Government of Canada in Ottawa.
As well, I think I would say this. Often, we hear the rhetoric from the government side about how we are a great, free enterprise government and we are going to free up the marketplace, then the next day we find out how it bailed out yet another business friend.
What we need is some consistency in policy. I am not being critical of the member. I think there is obviously a partnership that has to be developed. However, it has to be a consistent policy as well, and a blanket bailing out of its friends is no way to fund business opportunities and investments in Canada, nor is it any way to ensure that young people will be guaranteed those necessary jobs in the future.

Madam Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity of participating in this debate. I am very pleased to have the opportunity of responding to the hon. member's motion.
First, of course, I would be remiss if I did not congratulate the member on having brought this to the attention of the House. I think the member clearly recognizes that the young people are the foundation of Canada, our future prosperity and our competitiveness. Certainly the member also underscores that government has a role to play in helping our young people who will assume the responsibility for running this country in the years to come.
Let us talk for a minute about student unemployment, why we have unemployment and why there are these problems right now.
The simple answer would be that we entered a recession, the economic cycle turned downwards and a lot of Canadians, as a result, have lost their jobs or have
reduced employment opportunities. I think all of us will recognize and accept that as a fact.
However, it is time to move beyond that, and certainly beyond attributing blame, and ask some basic and fundamental questions, such as: "Why do we have a recession? What factors caused the recession to take place? Why could we not have avoided this economic trap?" We would have to answer that when the economic cycle started its downturn Canada did not have the resources necessary to combat it. We did not have budgetary surpluses. We did not have the tools at our disposal in order to prevent a recession from taking place in Canada.
When the economic downturn came and the inevitable hard times came we had no alternative but to suffer some body blows, some economic body blows.
We found ourselves, when the recession hit, as a country with a great deal of debt. As a result of that our interest rates were driven higher because we needed to keep refinancing this debt. It is an albatross around our necks. As a result, interest rates went up, which helped contribute to the economic downturn.
At the same time, the high debt also drove taxes higher. We have had a lot of tax increases in the last few years. Yes, middle class taxpayers are paying a very heavy load right now, but that direct increase in taxation is attributable almost directly and solely to the existence of a federal debt which keeps growing. The high debt, of course, is really nothing more than deferred taxes. This is basically my point.
We have a deficit today solely because we have a national debt. We are going to be paying $43 billion in interest this year on the debt alone. That wipes out the government's surplus and we do have a budgetary surplus now of almost $13 billion a year. We take in $13 billion a year more in taxes than we spend on programs, but that whole surplus is wiped out and an extra $30 billion of borrowing caused just because of the interest on the federal debt. This is the root behind our debate today. It is why we had a recession. It is why we could not avoid taking some measures to cushion ourselves from it. It is why we have student unemployment this particular summer.
We continue to go into debt in this country at the rate of $58,000 a minute and that is unacceptable.
June 10, 1991

As I mentioned a moment ago, a debt is actually deferred taxation. During the Debt Freedom Conference, which went on here in Ottawa, I noticed a statement by Laurent Thibeault, president of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. He said something pretty interesting: "A deficit is really a package of future taxes". He got it exactly right, it is. At that same conference, Michael Wilson, who was then the Minister of Finance, said: "Only if enough Canadians are prepared to speak out and express their views both forcefully and persistently can we build the genuine, political will to stop living beyond our means". That is the whole point of this, political will.
Right now we are, perhaps as a result of having enough political will, continuing an abominable process. We are continuing to steal the future through debts and deficits from our youth and that is not fair. It is generational theft. Imagine a young person who grew up in a fishing community, went to school there, went out and helped his father, his uncle and his family for years and years since he was 13 or 14 years old. Then he or she is told by the Government of Canada: "You have to go to Alberta to look for work because we are not allowed to give out any more licences, the reason being because there is not enough fish."
There are not enough fish. I have a letter here, written to the Government of the Soviet Union on March 22 of this year, to the U.S.S.R. Ministry of Fisheries, saying the following: "Initial quotas are allocated to the U.S.S.R. within the Canadian 200-mile zone in
1991-cod, redfish, turbot, squid, capelin, mackerel".
There are all of the tonnages listed off. Then, if I go to the other quota tables I will see Cuba and the Faeroe Islands, the group of islands off Denmark. They have quotas.
This year there is the G.D.R. I presume that is the German Democratic Republic which is now really the EEC, because it joined the EEC last year. There is Japan, Norway and Poland.
The question arises as to what is wrong with the Government of Canada that it would freeze every single young person in eastern Canada out of the fishing industry and say to him or her: "You are not allowed to fish anymore."
I have come to the conclusion that the Government of Canada has made the incredible mistake of concluding that fish do not swim. I say that because the government has given quotas to all these foreign nations on the basis that if it gives it to them off the Labrador coast: "They can do it up there because a lot of people are looking for licences off the Newfoundland coast."

June 10, 1991
Supply
The government assumes that by drawing lines in the middle of the Atlantic, every fish is going to stop when it gets to the line and it will never cross over the line.
It probably has the RCMP on the line saying: "You are not allowed to go any further". There is a stop sign somewhere. Maybe it has an electric fence that goes down through the middle of the Atlantic Ocean. The government believes that fish do not swim.
The other mistake it makes is by giving, for example, the Soviet Union a quota of capelin. It says: "Oh well, we are giving this to the Soviet Union because that capelin can only be caught in the fall when it is not roe bearing. It is not spawning". It says: "We leave the spawning capelin in the spring to Canadians. We reserve it for Canadians".
How can a Canadian catch a spawning capelin in the spring when the Soviet Union caught the non-spawning capelin in the fall?
The Government of Canada should reassess its policy of putting a total freeze on all licences for fishing in eastern Canada. It should reassess it on the basis that there is no logic or rationale that can be used.
The government is saying to a young person today in a fishing community that: "You, a young person in Canada, are not allowed ever to get a licence to pursue the occupation that your family has pursued for years", while at the same time, the young man can sit in the evening, look out on the ocean and see the lights of those foreign vessels offshore catching the very fish that he made an application to catch through the Government of Canada.
With those few remarks, I will take my seat. We are all expecting the minister of fisheries, of course, to change all of these decisions that were made two months ago by the Government of Canada and we are waiting for him to turn around, come into this House and say: "Look, we are going to allow Canadian youth to enter the fishing industry."
After all, we do not outlaw them from entering the legal profession or the medical profession, or from becoming a carpenter or a logger or a miner. But we outlaw them, we say: "You are not allowed to become a fisherman in this country". That is absolutely outrageous and outright discrimination against the youth of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with great care to the very distinguished member for Gander-Grand Falls here this afternoon raise this whole concern, and one he understands very well with respect to the fishing industry from that great province of Newfoundland, but he erred. He erred this afternoon, in my view, by suggesting that it is the fishery and the lack of fish or the policies of the Government of Canada with respect to fishing that has caused some demise to the youth who were neglected by this government.
Why did he not, one would wonder, bring forward so that everyone could hear the fact that this government is providing $40 million to Newfoundland alone for its youth on a five-year program. This is one of a kind in Canada other than, I believe, New Brunswick. It is providing $40 million with an agreement with their provincial government to, in fact, assist many young people with the problems that they face.
He is not the only one who understands the fisheries of this country, because the riding I represent has a large commercial fishing industry. It is one that the hon. member never even thought of with 1,200 commercial fishermen, and now experiencing some low catches as well as low prices.
The hon. member in front of me on this side of the House says: "You have fishermen?" Yes, 1200 commercial fishermen in one riding of mine alone.
It is not just the fishing industry. This government, which the hon. member failed to recognize, has with an agreement with that province come to the rescue of youth. Now he may say that is not enough, but if you were to compare that $40 million going by this government into the province of Newfoundland with other provinces, you would find it most lucrative.
I do not know if he is suggesting it should be doubled or the provincial government should also double. I do not know what he is suggesting. But to stand in his place here today and suggest that due to the policies with respect to some contracts going out to the Russians on some pregnant fish that they wanted to catch, and making a lot of fun about it, is not going to help the youth of Newfoundland, I don't suspect. How many may go out to fish and not stay in school, maybe become drop-outs because they have to assist in bringing home
June 10, 1991

some sustenance for their families? That may be a case in point.
This government clearly has done a great deal in an area he never even wanted to bring up in his comments this afternoon. He wanted to put it on the record. But $40 million is not something you can just flinch at and say is nothing.
I would like him to make a comment on that.

Mr. Speaker, I did not mention the money for summer student employment because I wanted to make one point about young people who are coming out of school. However, the hon. member has just mentioned it. I know his riding fairly well in Manitoba, and what he did not mention-of course, he said now they have a lucrative commercial fishery in fresh fish; that is absolutely correct-but I understand from talking to the Department of Fisheries personnel, is that they are claiming that this hon. member is actually making arrangements to have a company set up in his riding to process fish from Newfoundland and Nova Scotia. So he could go on and he could also mention that.
I will tell him now why I did not mention this $40 million. The change was made when this Conservative government took over. Before, under the Liberal administrations we had a great deal of money for non-profit organizations, for recreation groups and this sort of thing. A lot of this money that the hon. gentleman is talking about goes to private enterprise which now qualifies for the funds.
So we do see it. If the hon. member went over the list of jobs that he is talking about that are actually funded through private enterprise, he would see fast food take-out places funded for summer student employment. A lot of them, I maintain, would still hire the students regardless of whether the Government of Canada did it or not. Bartenders are funded for the summer under the Youth Employment Program. The bartender would have been hired anyway. It just shows the Conservative slant of this government in taking the youth employment money and redirecting it to where the jobs would have been anyway.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to join my
Supply
colleagues in responding to the hon. member's motion concerning youth employment.
In particular, I would like to focus my response on the Challenge program, the government's highly successful and innovative summer employment initiative for Canadian students which is now in its seventh year.
As I do so, I would like to not only relate the Challenge program on a national basis but also to draw comparisons with the Challenge program at work in my own riding of Fredericton-York- Sunbuiy during the current year.
What makes the Challenge program so successful is not just the thousands of summer jobs it provides young people; what makes it successful is the fact the various Challenge components offer meaningful work experience and positive reinforcement that will help participants meet the future demands of a highly competitive work force.
It is this far-sighted approach that has, in fact, defined this government's approach to all of our youth programs, be it Stay in School, Job Entry, elements of the labour force development strategy, the START program or many of the other initiatives designed with our young people's long-term employability in mind.
It is relatively easy for a government to haphazardly throw together so-called make work programs for young people every summer. But it is quite another thing to create a consistent co-ordinated program like Challenge, a program that generates employment opportunities that enhance the critical school-to-work transition, a program that attempts to address the long-term labour force market challenges faced not only by our youth but by employers as well.
Let there be no underestimating the scope of this challenge. Jobs are becoming more high tech and the educational requirements are getting stiffer almost as we speak. And yet while at least seven out of ten new jobs required in the 1990s and beyond will require at least 12 years of education, our entry labour pool population of 16- to 24-year-olds is actually diminishing. Clearly, if a third of a steadily shrinking labour force of youth lacks the necessary education or training for tomorrow's jobs, we have to ask: "Who is going to fill those jobs". If we cannot supply workers for the jobs of the future, we have to ask: "How will Canada ever compete in a global economy?"

June 10, 1991
Supply
It is in this context of squarely facing such urgent questions that the government has chosen to frame its youth initiatives. To simply throw money, as I have said, at short-term make-work programs that deal only with results instead of with causes would be irresponsible and finally disastrous. Because, simply put, if the school drop-out status quo is maintained and if the present low rate of on-the-job training continues, we as a country can look forward to decreased productivity, to decreased competitiveness and, finally, to a decreased standard of living.
That is why our youth initiatives focus on work experience, on career information and education, and on skill development. That is why we have targeted young people most at risk of leaving high school and those attempting to enter the labour market without having completed their education as the chief priorities.
That is also why we are emphasizing the development of human skill potential, the key ingredient to diversifying our economy, to competing globally and to creating jobs. That is why the Challenge program is so important.
The federal government is justifiably proud of the Challenge program. It combines work with education, creates thousands of summer jobs for students, fosters the leaming-by-doing concept, and forges partnerships in all sectors of the economy. It is a preventive program in every sense of the word, pro-active rather than re-active, a program designed to build for the future today. The various challenge options respond to a wide range of employment needs from assistance for students seeking entrepreneurial opportunities to counselling support for younger students looking to come to terms with their education and employment choices.
The Challenge program encourages employers to create jobs for students and help provide valuable work experience for Canada's future labour force. Employers take advantage of the program to assess the potential of their future employees.
Another positive element of the Challenge program is its adaptability, both regionally and in terms of its over all national emphasis. Therefore, over the past two years, the changing student employment situation has led us to shift our focus to provide more assistance to
those who have the most problems in the labour market. More emphasis has been placed on high school students, who traditionally have the most difficulty finding summer employment, as well as on potential and recent high school dropouts.
With this in mind, the government has increased funding for the SEED component of Challenge '91, while maintaining funding levels for all other challenge components.
In 1991, the Challenge Summer Student Employment Program will receive $143 million nationally with another $27.2 million allocated in ongoing funding to special youth strategy programs on a federal-provincial basis in both New Brunswick and Newfoundland.
In my riding of Fredericton-York-Sunbury this will amount to $1.1 million for the summer of 1991, plus an additional $1.8 million through the federal-provincial youth strategy during other portions of the 1991-92 year.
A moment ago I mentioned the Summer Employment Experience Development program, or SEED as it is called. I would like to take this opportunity to touch briefly on it and the various other challenge components.
In terms of resource allocation, SEED is the largest component of the Challenge program, receiving $80 million this year. SEED asks employers to create quality jobs for students and then subsidizes the students' wages for the summer. In my riding of Fredericton-York- Sunbury there is a total of $823,000 spent out of $1.1 million on the SEED program, which will enable 360 individual employers to engage for the summer 450 students. SEED is a very active, dynamic and important program in the Fredericton-York-Sunbury riding.
SEED has been a proven catalyst across the country for the creation of summer jobs that enable young people to contribute to society and that support the government's social priorities. Jobs in the areas of literacy, substance abuse, AIDS education, the environment and urban crime are therefore high on our eligibility list.
As well, this year's program will again encourage the hiring of visible minorities, aboriginal youth, disabled young people and the creation of activities designed to meet the needs of these groups.
June 10, 1991

The SEED program is divided into two streams, one for high school students starting jobs in late June or early July, and the other for college and university students for jobs normally starting in the month of May.
In 1990, high school students accounted for about 40 per cent of the SEED participants and female participation in the program reached 54 per cent.
Altogether, last summer SEED subsidized approximately 29,000 employers which created roughly 54,000 brand new jobs, many in the parts of the country hardest hit by student unemployment. I would like to repeat that the SEED program in 1991, this summer, will permit 350 employers in my riding to provide 450 students with summer work.
The second major component of the Challenge program is the Work Orientation Workshop or WOW program. In 1991, WOW will retain last year's funding level of $35.2 million across Canada. In my riding of Fredericton-York-Sunbury that figure for 1991 will be $275,000.
WOW is geared to the needs of our main target group, young people who are at risk of quitting school before they graduate. It encourages students to continue their education by providing work experience and life skills training.
WOW combines workshop counselling with practical on the job experience and academic support. This powerful combination is one of the most effective techniques for providing recent and potential drop-outs with new options for their future both in school and in the labour force.
In fact, so effective has the Work Orientation Workshop concept become that some WOW initiatives now run year-round. Last year in Canada nearly 16,000 young people participated in WOW projects. In 1991, in my riding of Fredericton-York-Sunbury between 120 and 150 students, depending upon the final calculations, will participate in these Workshop Orientation programs which have been so effective, both nationally and in every local riding.
A pivotal co-ordinating element of the Challenge program is the network of Canada Employment Centres for students, which will receive $9.7 million this year. There are approximately 420 of these student placement
Supply
offices right across the country. During the summer months they help students find jobs and help employers locate workers. The Canada Employment Centre for students offers a free placement service for employers. There is no charge for listing a job vacancy.
I am pleased to say that the Canada Employment Centre for students is fully utilized and fully at work in my riding of Fredericton-York-Sunbury.
In 1990 the Canada Employment Centres recorded more than 270,000 student placements across Canada. That is very fine work. Excellent results for a specialized student employment centre.
The fourth component of Challenge is the business drive for jobs. Our partners are the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, the Retail Council of Canada and business members across the country. The core of this program is business talking to business about the benefits of hiring students. This year the funding contribution to that program will be $805,000 to provide financial and advertising support. That is also a very effective and very important program.
Finally, there is the Native Internship Program to which the Challenge program will contribute $2.3 million in 1991. In my riding of Fredericton-York-Sunbury that figure will be $64,300 and will employ 15 students in 10 government departments.
The Native Internship Program provides aboriginal students with valuable work experience at Employment and Immigration Canada offices and in other departments across the country.
Last summer in Canada almost 500 native students benefited from participation in this program.
In reviewing these Challenge components, it is clear that the common link is relevance to both student and labour market needs. It is clear too, from the feedback the government receives every year from students and employers alike that this approach to summer work is the right one, particularly in light of Canada's competitive priorities for the 1990s.
Through the Challenge program, not only do we encourage students to stay in school, but we also give them a chance to acquire the experience and the skills they will need to find jobs in Canada's future workforce. Employers for their part benefit from the nurturing of an efficient and dynamic labour force.

June 10, 1991
Supply
The hon. member's concern with employment in this motion and with the prospects for the summer of Canadian young people is a concern all members of this House and certainly this government share. It is a concern that this government is clearly committed to addressing through focused and effective programs such as the Challenge program and the components of it which I have described, all of which have long-term implications for our youth and for our labour market as a whole.

speakeroldname: Mr. Marcel R. Tbemblay (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Minister of State (Youth) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Youth); Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have often heard members in this House blaming our government for inadequate policies.
Today, I would like to correct that impression. Our government is constantly rethinking its youth assistance policies. More than ever, the government wants to show our kids how to grow their own food instead of increasing their dependency by feeding them.
Government funding for youth programs has not diminished. We are simply trying to do better with the same amount of money. We try to encourage our private sector partners, business people and community agencies to take charge of the labour market with our support.
The government has a new approach. We do not want to create local jobs that would lead to youth assistance dependency; instead we want to help our young people by making their transition to the labour market easier. Why should we key on paying for jobs which would exist anyway?
There is no need to create jobs for just about anyone. Several workers are able to find jobs without government assistance. So, our government chooses to keep its funding for the most needy. Our initiatives are future-oriented. We opt for more preventive measures. The stay-in-school project is a good example.
Other programs will follow to help prepare our kids to meet tomorrow's challenge. I have a question for my hon. colleague about the stay-in-school project.
The opposition has talked a lot about summer jobs for students. This is the objective of one of several youth programs, but programming for summer student jobs does not help the 30 per cent of Canadian youth who drop out.
My question: Can the member tell the House what concrete steps the government is taking to assist youth to stay in school.

Madam Speaker, the government recognizes that unemployment can lead to very severe social problems and that the greatest at-risk component of our student population is, as the hon. member says, the close to 30 per cent who will not finish high school.
One very significant program which has been introduced on a pilot basis, an experimental basis in Newfoundland and in New Brunswick to which I have referred, is the youth strategy through which year-round access offices have been established. Counselling services have been established to encourage young people who are out of school or contemplating leaving school to review their future, to come to terms with education requirements and to come to terms with their future in the job market.
In my riding of Fredericton-York-Sunbury, that youth strategy will have a total application of almost $2.3 million in the 1991 year, of which about $275,000, or 10 per cent, will be attributed to the workshop orientation program in the summer.

June 10, 1991

That is a federal-provincial shared program, 70 per cent supported by the federal government and 30 per cent by the provincial government. I think the program in Newfoundland is similar, although I do not have the exact details.
All I can say is that is one very dramatic initiative which this government has taken in company with the province of New Brunswick and the province of Newfoundland to address that very specific area to which my hon. friend refers.
The WOW programs which I have described in my address, while they are summer work programs, also address the prospective high school dropout with the combination of on-the-job experience, counselling and training with a view to returning to high school to complete education and then on to the job opportunities which have been identified through the WOW experience, frequently on a permanent basis.

Madam Speaker, on a point of order. I see by the clock that we have about 20 minutes and by prior agreement we would have the 20 minutes on our side to speak. We have two members who are going to speak, and I just wanted to advise the Chair that they would each be taking the 10 minutes. I do not know how that would work with regard to the questions after they speak but I would ask your indulgence and the indulgence of the House, seeing as both these members have done a great deal of preparation, to get them both on.
