Madam Speaker, I would also like to say a few words on this very important resolution put down by my friend and my colleague from Welland-St. Catharines-Thorold. I suppose of the many issues that we have the opportunity of debating in the House, none is more important than the substance of the resolution which my colleague and friend has put before us today. It calls upon this government to implement measures immediately to
Supply
alleviate the devastatingly high rate of unemployment amongst Canadian youth.
I know the House has heard it several times today, but I thought having listened to my friend from Fredericton-York-Sunbury that it was time again to remind the House of what the resolution says. I say to him that I listened with great care to what he had to say and for the most part nobody on this side will argue with what he said. There are some things he did not say that I would have liked to hear him say, but I will not put words in his mouth. In his talking about the Challenge program and how good it is, and the Work Orientation Workshop and how good it is, we do not argue with that. We argue, we take exception, to the way the government has tried to gut these programs, to use a good Newfie expression. We take exception to the manner in which, in real terms, the government has taken what has the potential to be a good program and rendered it impotent by not giving it the amount of money that it needs to function effectively and to reach those thousands of people out there, young people, who are on the unemployment rolls.
He read his speech well. It is a marvellous idea he pushes, and we support the same idea. He stopped short by not telling us what he is doing on behalf of the people of Fredericton-York-Sunbury, and by extension the people of Canada, to beat some sense into the thinking of this government that this is not a time to renege. His own words condemn his argument when he says the WOW program has the same amount of money that it had last year. Implicit is the admission that in effect there is a cutback. Everybody out there knows that with inflation, if you have only the same amount of money as you had last year, you have to cut back somewhere. His own statement gives a lie to the argument he tries to make. His own statement tells us that there is, in real terms, not as much money in this program or in other programs as there was last year.
The reason we bring forward this motion today is because youth unemployment, the whole area we focused on today, for all the rhetoric, for all the brave speech-making on the other side, has become a wasteland. It is an economic nightmare when you realize what is happening to the talent, to the potential and to the skills out there vested in those young people. It is the pillaging of a resource. Our most valuable and precious resource is being wilfully pillaged by this government.

June 10, 1991
Supply
There can be no other explanation for it. The government is pillaging, devastating, brow-beating and pummelling our most valuable and precious resource. What is happening here is a human tragedy. It is a double tragedy that men and women on the other side will stand up and try to condone what is going on here, try to put a good face on it and try to pretend that disaster somehow is a success. It is a human tragedy of considerable magnitude.
The youth jobs are drying up. The tuition rates are going up in the universities. The students' ability to even get an education is being further limited by this government with the cutbacks and the freeze, first for two years and now up to five years in transfer payments.
Consider that in the province that I come from, the province of Newfoundland and Labrador, the unemployment rate according to the Statistics Canada figures for April, 1991, was 33.5 per cent. One-third or one out of every three young Newfoundlanders 18 to 24 is walking around, not because he or she is lazy, not because he or she will not go to work, but because there is no work to go to.
Those programs that my friend from Fredericton- York-Sunbury made reference to a few minutes ago could help bridge the gap for some of those people if the government had not been so niggardly, stingy, or deliberate in its plan. I say deliberate because I see in the government's approach to youth unemployment the latest indication of its brutal and single-minded consistency. This government always hits the most vulnerable. Look around you. Look at what it has done for the aged and for the sick in terms of the cutbacks in transfer payments for health. Look at what it has done to children in terms of family allowance payments. Look at rural people in terms of rural post office closures and railway abandonments and so on. Look at small business, the most vulnerable in any sector. In business it is the small business. In society generally it is rural as opposed to urban. Among humans it is children as opposed to adults. It is the aged as opposed to others. It is the sick as opposed to the healthy.
This government, you would think with deliberate intent, sat down with a pencil and said: "Okay, who is the worst off out there, who can we hit, who is most
vulnerable?" In its exercise it came across students, students who were already having difficulty staying in college to complete their education so they would be better off. This is the crowd that preaches training and preaches qualification and it has cut those students off at the knees, those very students who want to get qualified. It has cut them off with higher tuition fees and other expenses which make university almost impossible for many of them.
This government has a brutal consistency. It goes out there and it hits those who are most vulnerable. In this present example, it hits the students, the young people, whose rate of unemployment, particularly in Newfoundland as I have said, is one-third in the age group 18 to 24.
This government is brutally, brutally consistent. It kicks you while you are down. The students are down right now, the young people are down, the 18 to 24 age group is down because of the economy and down because of increased expenses of going on to college and continuing their education. These people are down and out.
So what does this government do? It is consistent all right. It kicks you while you are down and now it kicks the student.
In the same vein it turns a blind eye, it turns a deaf ear because it cannot be argued that those students' plight has not been put on the floor of this House of Commons. It cannot be argued that the government does not know what the problem is. The government has symbolically shown that it understands very well what the problem is because it has crafted programs to deal with the problem, but then it will not fund those programs. It will not fund them adequate to the need.
I say again to my friend from New Brunswick that the WOW program and the Challenge program are marvellous programs.
You will not find anybody on this side of the House knocking the programs as concepts, as workable functional utilitarian ideas. Our plea is for the government to literally put its money where its mouth is. If it cares as much about youth unemployment as its spokespeople have said today it does, let it put more money into those particular programs.
June 10,1991

In conclusion, I reinforce what my friend from Welland-St. Catharines-Thorold has so well said in his speech today. The time has come for the government to implement immediately some measures to cure this problem before it becomes an overwhelming and consuming tragedy. The loss will be ours if we lose the skills the potential and the future of those tens and thousands of young people who are out there walking around because they would just like to have some work to go to.

have a couple of comments on the hon. member's speech. He talks about the funding for post-secondary education. I suspect that he does not really have the latest figures in terms of the percentage of government funding for post-secondary education that is now held by the Government of Canada.

Adjournment Debate

Madam Speaker, to the second part of the question, the member well knows that none of us in the speeches today has said that the programs that are implemented are all bad. We recognize, as I said in my speech, that the WOW program, the Challenge program, the youth strategy, the kinds of things to which he makes reference are all good programs. They are not adequately funded but they are good concepts.
What do you do to keep them in school? I am sony I do not have more time to answer more extensively, but in a word of response to the gentleman who raised the question "What do you do to keep them in school?"-I also answered that in my speech-you make tuition fees affordable so they can go in the first place.

Madam Speaker, I would simply like to address one of the effects of cuts made in the summer job creation programs in my riding.

It goes exactly to the question just asked by the previous member in that these cuts in summer employment are going to guarantee that many poor children do not go back to school this fall. Many poor children whose only means of getting through the summer, having a little bit of job experience, and feeling the value of going back to school in September has been lost to them.
I have thousands of families in my riding who live below the poverty level and these are the families who are not able to benefit this year from the Challenge '91 program because the funding for this program was cut from over $100,000 just two years ago to $22,000 for the last two years.
With so little time, I would like to read into the record what happens to children who live in poverty when they do not get a chance for a summer job that gives them a little bit of income which allows their family to send them back to school in the fall. What happens is that poverty is perpetuated.
I want to read from an article in today's Ottawa Citizen about the results of that poverty: "Chronic illness is substantially higher among children who live below the poverty line than those who live above. It has double the number of psychiatric disorders for those who live in
poverty compared to those who do not. At school poor performance is twice as high for children on welfare as for children not on welfare". The dropout rate is approximately four and a half to five times as high for poor children as it is for non-poor children and, most devastating of all, accidental deaths are nine to one for poor children. Homicide-suicide is four to one for poor children. Pedestrian car accidents that kill children are two and a half times as high if you are poor.
These are the results of poverty. These are the results of not having summer employment. These are the results of not going to school and perpetuating the whole cycle of poverty.
I say to the last speaker who asked the question that the way to keep young people in school, the way to end the cycle of poverty is to have enough family income so that people feel they have some hope of a better future.

Madam Speaker, on May 17,1 asked the government what it was going to do to help the 1,600 employees who lost their jobs as a result of the Pascal Hardware bankruptcy. I pointed out that Pascal's hardware had been in business in Montreal and region for 87 years and as a result of its bankruptcy on May 16, 21 stores were closed and 1,600 employees lost their jobs.
In particular, I asked if this lay-off and these workers would qualify under the Program for Older Worker Adjustment, known as POWA. I also asked what other initiatives the government would take to retrain and re-employ the 1,600 individuals.

June 10, 1991

POWA, the Program for Older Worker Adjustment, is good in principle, but very defective in its criteria and its administration. And it is under-funded.
I have here an article from The Winnipeg Free Press of May 23, by Leonard Shifrin who calls the POWA program "a cruel lottery for the laid off" and he points out that "while this program promised much, after three years it has only spent $73 million of the promised $150 million used in the first two years and it only provided benefits to 2,244 ex-workers". Right across the country only 2,234 workers, when at Pascal's alone, 1,600 have lost their jobs. Obviously, no matter if this program is good in concept, it is grossly, grossly under-funded. I hope that Pascal's employees will qualify under that program. The program needs to be extended.
This bankruptcy of Pascal's also raises several other issues. One is that the Bankruptcy Act needs amendment. Under the present Bankruptcy Act, employees only have the right to receive $500 in back wages and after that they become unsecured creditors, so all sorts of other creditors get their money before employees, some of whom have worked for 20 and 30 years. I know some of them who worked at Pascal's. They are going to get a raw deal after many, many years of working for that company.
I think this bankruptcy also gives rise to questions to the government as to when is it going to come forward with amendments to the Bankruptcy Act.
Finally, I hope, as I said, that the government will announce that Pascal's employees will qualify for POWA. I hope, as well, that the government will realize that POWA is not enough. In addition to more funding for POWA and some amendments to its program, it must also bring amendments to the Bankruptcy Act to give laid-off employees, as a result of a bankruptcy, much more compensation for their wages so they should not be left out in the dark, as they will be under this program.
I anxiously await the response of the minister or the parliamentary secretary.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ken James (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to thank the hon. Warren Allmand for his question concerning the lay-off at J. Pascal Inc. and its potential for consideration under the Program for Older Workers Adjustment, or
Adjournment Debate
POWA, and what the government initiatives are with respect to retraining and re-employing these workers.
As the hon. member is aware, POWA is a federal-provincial and territorial program designed to help long-service older workers who have been permanently laid off and have no prospect of finding other employment. Lay-offs that occur in all private sector industries and commercial Crown corporations, including the lay-off at J. Pascal Inc., are eligible for consideration under POWA and subject to the criteria consistently with other lay-offs across the country. I would stress, however, that POWA remains a program of last resort, to be applied after all other adjustment measures have been considered.
With respect to the hon. member's concern regarding the consideration under POWA of the lay-off that occurred at J. Pascal Inc., I would like to reassure him that it will be assessed by the Canada-Quebec and Canada-Ontario POWA committees.
While this analysis takes place, most laid-off employees will be provided with financial assistance through the unemployment insurance program. Once the analysis is complete, Mr. Andre Bourbeau, Quebec Minister of Manpower, Income Security and Skills Development and the hon. Bob MacKenzie, Ontario Minister of Labour and the Minister of Labour, the hon. Marcel Danis, will evaluate the findings to determine whether the lay-off is eligible under the program for older worker adjustment.
For your information, I would like to take this opportunity to outline the main lay-off eligibility criteria. Veiy significant economic disruption in the region; significant loss of employment in the industry; importance of the lay-off relative to the size of the community and a large proportion of older workers affected are some of the criteria.
I would like to refer the member to the information I have passed on to him, and we want to thank him very much for his concern.

Madam Speaker, when I was a kid, every day after school, I and my friends would go down to the cliffs on the edge of the Don River Valley in Toronto to play.

June 10, 1991
Adjournment Debate
We would not only play on the cliffs but we would play in the dumps that were all along the edge of those cliffs. Today, Madam Speaker, you and I would not call them dumps, we would call them land-fill sites.
All those dumps or land-fill sites are now completely filled up. There is no place else to put garbage in those locations. They are all grassed over, and that is a real problem.
Ten years ago when I served on metropolitan Toronto council, and on the executive committee there, we bought a huge land-fill site, the Keele Valley site, just north of Toronto in Maple, Ontario.
We were told at the time that this would last for my lifetime and probably for the lifetime of my children as well. Today, we are told that at the end of this year, at the end of 1991, that land-fill site is going to be completely filled up. There is not going to be any space in it at all any more.
We are told as well that by 1993 the last remaining land-fill site in metropolitan Toronto will be completely filled. There is no place else to put garbage.
Metropolitan Toronto is not the only place with this problem. Every large municipality has this problem whether in Ontario, Quebec or the prairies. We are told that by the middle of the 1990s all of these existing land-fill sites are going to be completely filled up because we in Canada have the dubious distinction of being considered the most wasteful people on the face of the earth.
Canadians produce 1.7 kilograms of garbage per person per day. That compares with the Americans at 1.5, the Germans at 1.3 and the Chinese at less than .5. In fact, every Canadian produces about one tonne of garbage each year. Two-thirds of all of that comes from industry, business and institutions. The other third comes from our own homes. About 30 to 50 per cent of all that garbage and waste that comes from our own homes comes from packaging.
What are we going to do about this? Some people say: "Let's incinerate it. Let's burn it all". Other people say: "Let's ship it out of town". In Toronto we say: "Let's ship it to Kirkland Lake". In Montreal they say: "Let's ship it to Sept ties". Other people say: "Let's just let it pile up. There is no problem at all. Let's go on and
continue the garbage binge". Other people say: "We should be recycling it". And some people say: "We should be reducing it". In fact, that is really what we should be doing.
Since packaging is such a large part of that waste, the federal government, with tougher regulations, can play an important part in reducing that packaging that is filling up our land-fill sites and causing us this great problem.
The green plan says that we are going to do this voluntarily. We are going to cut down on packaging voluntarily until some time in 1992. Then, after that, we will start to think about putting some regulations in place in 1993 if that does not work. By that time, all of these sites are going to be filled and it will be too late.
I say to the minister tonight: "For heaven's sakes, Mr. Minister, do not wait until we have to pile up the garbage in our parks, school yards and apartment balconies. Let's get some tough regulations in there right now."

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Belsher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and Minister for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to address my remarks to the hon. member for Don Valley East concerning packaging of waste.
He is so right in saying that the largest single component of municipal solid waste in Canada, accounting for some 30 per cent of the total, is in packaging. The importance of this issue is underscored in Canada's Green Plan, which he has already acknowledged.
The National Packaging Protocol is the first initiative cited in the green plan in the list of Canada's efforts to reduce waste. Under the National Packaging Protocol an over-all target was established of a 50 per cent reduction in packaging waste by the year 2000. The in-term targets of 20 per cent by the year 1992 and 35 per cent by 1996 were also set.
The federal and provincial environment departments, as expressed by the Canadian Council of Ministers of the Environment, fully support these goals and consider voluntary compliance as the preferred means of achievement. Regulations to achieve those targets will be implemented if voluntary action, especially by industry, fails to achieve the 1992 goal of a 20 per cent reduction in packaging.

June 10, 1991

Under this front, through the National Packaging Thsk Force, the Canadian Council of Ministers of the Environment is engaged in developing recommendations for a comprehensive federal-provincial legislative package to support the objectives of the National Packaging Protocol. The recommended legislative elements will contain standards and codes for packaging and specified content and composition for packaging materials. In fact, dialogue has already begun with the task force multistakeholder group to develop its regulatory framework, including the development of examples of model regulations at the federal and provincial levels. Discussion and consultation will also be required to ensure a consistent application of the legislative elements throughout Canada.
Establishing regulations is only one of the possible means to achieve the goals of the National Packaging Protocol. Environment Canada will participate in the investigation of possible economic instruments and other means to support the protocol's objectives of reducing waste and protecting Canada's environment.

Madam Speaker, I would like to thank the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance for giving me the opportunity to continue this debate on the importance of fiscal transfers to the provinces.
The question raised last week in the House of Commons during Question Period was prompted by a report by the very well respected National Council on Welfare. In its Spring 1991 report entitled Funding Health and Higher Education-Danger Looming it raises the alarm that perhaps Canadians were not aware of just how dramatic the changes were that were about to take place within the funding. Although they did not use any particularly derogatory or nasty adjectives that perhaps the opposition would be more inclined to use to accurately describe the government, they did, however, note just how cash poor the provinces are going to be. Provinces such as Nova Scotia with hard-done-by areas such as Cape Breton deserve more support than they appear to be getting and will get in the future.
Adjournment Debate
They start out with the proposition that health care and post- secondary education are undertakings vital to the well-being of Canadians. I think even the government could agree with that. They continue to stress the fact that people in poorer provinces would have to make do with health care services that are inferior to the services enjoyed by Canadians who happen to live in richer provinces. In other words, people living in Cape Breton, rural Quebec, northern Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, interior parts of B.C. would be hard pressed to keep up the medical services and post-secondary education if the present strategy of the federal government were allowed to take place.
That, by the way, is the reason why this party opposes so strenuously Bill C-20, which is its budgetary strategy for reducing even further the payments. So as bad as this story is from the National Council of Welfare, I can assure you that it will even be worse if Bill C-20 is allowed to pass through this House.
This report is not a negative report. They in fact have several recommendations which I would like to bring to the attention of the House. These recommendations should be taken more seriously by the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister, in a very offhand response said: "Oh, the report is inadequate", and sat back down. However, the report like all reports can be discussed intelligently, and that is why I am happy to have the government here tonight. To say it is inadequate when this organization has a 20-year history of presenting Canadians with well thought out positions on poverty, issues that most Canadians would not like to hear about, or at least most governments would not like to hear about. These people have continued to work hard on behalf of Canadians and deserve not to be dismissed in that easy way.
It recommended that the federal government should continue to play a significant financial role in both health care and post-secondary education. Can you imagine, in this country, that recommendation having to be made? Can you imagine not taking it for granted that the federal government has a role in medicare and a role in post-secondary education?
The very fact that the organization thought that it had to remind the government is a testimony to how much things have changed in the last while.

June 10, 1991
Adjournment Debate
Second, any changes in the financing of health and higher education should result from federal-provincial negotiations rather than being imposed by Ottawa. How did this government ever win an election? It won an election by saying: "Look at what the Liberals are doing. They are imposing on this country".
This most respected organization says: "The imposition of terrible measures by this very government". It has quickly forgotten just how important this is.
There are many other issues raised in this report.
I stand here before the House asking the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance to reconsider their responses, to not describe the report as being inadequate but stand up and understand that Canadians are expecting more from them in terms of fiscal transfers.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Barbara Sparrow (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague from Winnipeg North Centre. We had the privilege of working together for the last two and a half years on industry, science and technology, so I look forward to our work together on health and welfare.
Canadians do love their health care. Each and every one of us do. There have been a number of public opinion polls that indicate a very high approval rating. Actually about 90 per cent believe that our medicare system makes Canada one of the best countries in the world in which to live.
However, it is also recognized that health expenditures are increasing. They are increasing faster than the rate of inflation and the growth rate of the Canadian population.
In such an environment where provinces today spend up to one-third of their budgets on health, provincial finance ministers are naturally very concerned about over all costs. It is now generally accepted that spending more on health care does not always result in proportionate improvements in the state of health care.
Major transfers to the provinces, including both the cash and the tax transfers, will grow on average by 3.7 per cent for the period 1991-92 to 1995-96. All other federal programs will grow by 3.4 per cent.
This government stands by the national standards of our medicare system. The Minister of National Health
and Welfare has made this clear in the House. This is not a promise that the government takes lightly, as a recent National Council on Welfare report would have one to believe. We are very serious about our national medicare system. Poverty does affect Canadians and it is also a major concern for this government.
This is definitely an issue which requires more time, more effort and more attention from all Canadians.
Since 1984, the government has embarked on a series of initiatives to improve the situation of Canadian families. Our approach has been to support self-sufficiency among Canadians through economic and social policies which have helped to create a climate in which job creation can prosper. Even in a time of necessary fiscal restraint, however, the government has acted to better support lower income families with children and this government has increased by more than 50 per cent the maximum value of the child tax credit since 1984. We introduced a new child tax credit system. We have helped parents who are separated or divorced with their maintenance fees and we introduced a goods and services tax credit under the GST.

Madam Speaker, I rise this evening with regard to a question I put forward on May 30, 1991, to the Minister of Employment and Immigration concerning the contradictions in public documents that have been released regarding the Al-Mashat case. I wish to put on record the words of the former President of the United States, John F. Kennedy. He submitted to Congress a special message on ethical conduct in government which reads as follows:
No responsibility of government is more fundamental than the responsibility of maintaining the highest standards of ethical behaviour by those who conduct the public business. There can be no dissent from the principle that all officials must act with unwavering integrity, absolute impartiality, and complete devotion to the public interest. This principle must be followed not only in reality but in appearance. For the basis of effective Government is public confidence, and that confidence is endangered when ethical standards falter or appear to falter.
June 10, 1991

It would be very helpful if the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration could share with members of the House this evening an explanation with regard to the contradictions between version A and version B of public documents that have been made available concerning the Al-Mashat case.
Canadians are concerned about how an individual of such stature as Al-Mashat could get into the country when there are thousands upon thousands of people who are waiting, and have been waiting for quite some time, to obtain admission to Canada.
Canadians expect more, much more from their elected officials. Contradictions and half-truths are simply unacceptable to the people of this country. They want the issues of our time addressed with clarity, common sense, single-mindedness, and sincerity of purpose. They want high standards of ethical behaviour maintained by those who conduct the public business. I suggest to the parliamentary secretary that they want performance from this government, not public relations, and they want leadership, not salesmanship. I hope that the parliamentary secretary to the minister can provide a suitable answer.

speakeroldname: Mr. Francis G. LeBIanc (Cape Breton Highlands- Canso):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to begin by thanking the parliamentary secretary for his patience.
On Monday, June 3, I had occasion to rise in this House during Question Period and ask the minister of fisheries about the alleged illegality of the dockside monitoring program.
The government is currently compelling fishermen and fish processors to pay user fees to private companies set up by the government to monitor the catches of fishermen as a condition of entering into a licensing agreement with the ministry of fisheries.
The problem is that the government did not bother to obtain either legislative or regulatory authority for the user fee portion of the program. That was the finding of the senior legal counsel of the Parliamentary Joint Committee on the Scrutiny of Regulations and Statutory Instruments.
In his report, which I released on May 22, the senior legal counsel states: "The minister, in using his discretion to obtain the payment of monitoring fees to monitoring companies by fishermen and to secure the fishermen's signature of agreements, is exercising his power unlawfully".
I sent a copy of this report to the minister of fisheries on the day it was released. On that day we also heard from the parliamentary secretary that the user fee portion of the program was under review by his ministry. I would have thought that the result of that review, given the thorough and authoritative way in which the document presented the case for the illegality of the fees, would have convinced the minister of fisheries to do the honourable thing and to rescind the user fees and reimburse the fishermen. Perhaps if he were insistent on imposing these user fees, he would have sought the necessary legislative authority to do so at a later date. However, when I asked the question of the minister of

June 10, 1991
Adjournment Debate
fisheries a week ago today, his reaction was to slough off the report as just one lawyer's opinion.
For the minister to assume this stance shows not only a callous disregard for the law, but something which we would not have expected from a minister of his experience and his calibre. The minister of fisheries appears to hope that no one will take this matter any further. He seems to hope the government will get away with this blatant disregard for the law, even though the program has clearly been brought into question with regard to its illegality.
This is no way to deal with the enormous problems facing the fisheries. For the government to resort to illegality or to coverting the legal requirements to bring about its objective is all the more galling to fishermen who are forced to take food off their families' tables in order to pay for these ludicrous user fees. Fishermen are tired of the government ignoring this fact and claiming that the program is in the best interests of fishermen and everyone involved in the fisheries. They are not fooled, they are appalled. They are demanding that the government confront the issue of these illegal fees head on and not sit back smugly but re-evaluate its program, rescind those fees and reimburse the fishermen who had been asked to pay them without the proper legislative authority.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Belsher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and Minister for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Thank you very much, Madam Speaker. The Dockside Monitoring Program was introduced as a pilot project in 1989 with the support of the industry to reduce the widespread misreporting and under-reporting of catches in the Gulf of St. Lawrence. This program, which was expanded in 1990 and 1991 to cover all mobile groundfish vessels, as well as mid-shore crab vessels, shrimp vessels and large herring seiners, will continue. The legal opinions regarding the legality of collecting dockside monitoring fees referred to by the
member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso have been reviewed by the legal counsel to the Department of Fisheries and Oceans.
The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans continues to hold the position, based on past legal advice, that he has the authority to implement the current system and to require fishermen to pay the costs of the monitoring program. The fishermen as well as producers on the Atlantic coast who benefit from the fish resources have indicated that they want a system which will maintain an orderly and an economically viable fishery. The Dockside Monitoring Program is a tool which is critical to the realization of this goal. It ensures that management's plans are implemented fairly and the high quality of data gathered under the program also aids in stock assessment, ensuring that the total allowable catches, the TACs, are set based on actual stock strength. Over time, this will help the stocks to recover.
Furthermore, with the introduction of individual quotas on groundfish, crab and shrimp fisheries in the gulf, it becomes critical to have a precise and timely monitoring system in place. The fishermen and processors who benefit from the resource must contribute to its management and rebuilding. The Department of Fisheries and Oceans does not have sufficient resources to pay for the program. This is not to say that the program cannot be improved. Consultations will be held this year with industry groups to discuss ways in which the efficiency of the program can be improved and cost minimized.
I wish to thank the hon. member for bringing this again to our attention.
